META.subtitleDoc: CBE Phenomenon-Driven Lesson Sequence — Sub-Strand 3.1 (8 Lessons)

UNIT.subject: Essential Mathematics
UNIT.content:
• Ungrouped data
• Frequency distribution tables for discrete data
• Mean, mode and median of ungrouped data
• Application of graphs of data
• Representing data using bar graphs, line graphs and pie charts
• Interpreting data from bar graphs, line graphs and pie charts
• Representing data on a digital device
• Project: collecting, organising, representing and interpreting data to guide school or community decisions
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) draw a frequency distribution table for ungrouped data
b) determine mean, mode and median of ungrouped data
c) represent data using bar graphs, line graphs and pie charts
d) interpret data from bar graphs, line graphs and pie charts
e) appreciate the importance of data organization and interpretation in making effective decisions
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Critical thinking and problem solving: the learner develops interpretation and inference skills when collecting data, building frequency tables and drawing conclusions from graphs and charts.
• Digital literacy: the learner develops the skills of connecting and interacting with digital technology when using digital devices to draw graphs and charts to represent the data collected.
UNIT.values:
• Integrity: the learner displays honesty while working in groups and collecting data, such as when making frequency distribution tables.
• Love: the learner is considerate of others when working with peers to extract information from graphs and charts and draw conclusions.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking questions and defining problems: learners ask what a school transport pattern or a favourite-colour poll can tell us and what data is needed to answer it.
• Analyzing and interpreting data: learners organise data in frequency tables, compute mean, median and mode, and read graphs and charts to find patterns.
• Using mathematics and computational thinking: learners calculate averages, convert frequencies to pie chart angles and use digital tools to plot graphs.
• Developing and using models: learners build a cumulative data model (table, statistics and graphs) that is revised as new evidence arrives.
• Engaging in argument from evidence: learners defend recommendations to the school using their graphs and statistics.
• Obtaining, evaluating and communicating information: learners present findings and critique how others have represented data.
UNIT.pcis: • Life Skills (Decision Making): the learner makes informed decisions when identifying patterns from the graphs and charts and drawing conclusions.
UNIT.careers:
• Journalism and media: reporting and presenting data-driven stories with graphs and charts.
• Sports management and coaching: analysing player statistics such as race times and match scores of Kenyan athletes.
• Hospitality industry: tracking customer preferences and sales of items such as mandazi, tea and nyama choma.
• Sole proprietorship (kiosk or market stall trading): using sales data to decide what stock to buy.
• Guidance and counselling: using survey data to understand learners' needs.
• Photography and creative arts: using audience data to guide planning.
UNIT.focus: This unit uses real data from the learners' own school, such as how they travel to school and which food or colour they prefer, to show why organising and interpreting data matters. Learners progress from frequency tables to mean, median and mode, then to bar graphs, line graphs and pie charts, finishing with a data project that guides a real decision in the school or community. Each lesson follows Predict, Observe, Explain, Driving Question Board and Model Building phases, with a class data model revised cumulatively.
UNIT.phenomenon: The school principal must decide how to use limited resources: whether to arrange a school bus route, build a bicycle shed, or add a second lunch serving. Different learners give conflicting opinions: 'Almost everyone walks', 'Most of us come by matatu', 'The bus is always full'. Students collect real data on how their class travels to school (walking, matatu, boda boda, bicycle, private car, school bus) and see a long, confusing list of 40 responses where nobody can say who is right. Once the same data is organised into a frequency table and shown as a bar graph and pie chart, the answer becomes clear, yet the mean, median and mode tell slightly different stories. The puzzle: how can the same raw list of numbers seem meaningless in one form and decisive in another, and which summary or graph should the principal trust?
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• Two Kenyan athletes have race times for five 800 m races; one has the faster mean but the other is more consistent, so which is the better pick for the Kericho county team?
• A mandazi seller in Kisumu records daily sales for a week; a line graph shows a sharp rise on market day that the total alone hides.
• A newspaper pie chart of how a Nairobi family spends its monthly income (rent, food, school fees, transport, savings) leads to different conclusions depending on how the slices are read.
• The class tallies tree types in the school compound (grevillea, cypress, eucalyptus, jacaranda) and the frequency table reveals which species dominates before anyone counts them again.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: How can we turn a messy list of data from our school into clear evidence that helps our principal make a fair decision?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. How do we use statistics in day-to-day life?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1: Anchoring phenomenon. Learners predict how the class travels to school, collect raw data, and see that the unorganised list does not settle the principal's question. The Driving Question Board is launched.
Lesson 2: Frequency distribution tables. Learners use tally marks to build a frequency table for discrete data (travel mode, favourite colour, tree types in the compound) and compare it with the raw list.
Lesson 3: Mode and mean. Learners predict the 'typical' value, then compute the mode and mean from the frequency table for ungrouped data such as the number of siblings or shoe sizes.
Lesson 4: Median and comparing measures. Learners order the data, find the median, and discuss when mean, median or mode best represents the data (for example Kenyan athletes' race times).
Lesson 5: Bar graphs and line graphs. Learners draw bar graphs for categories and line graphs for change over time (daily mandazi sales), and discuss which graph fits which kind of data.
Lesson 6: Pie charts. Learners convert frequencies to angles, draw pie charts of the school travel data and family budgets, and compare representations for the principal's question.
Lesson 7: Interpreting graphs and charts and using digital tools. Learners in pairs extract information, draw and defend conclusions, spot misleading graphs, and recreate graphs on a digital device.
Lesson 8: Project and consolidation. Learners present data-based recommendations to the principal, revise the class model of how data becomes evidence, and return to the DQB to answer the driving question.

LESSONS.title: Whose Claim Is Right? Launching the Principal's Problem
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (1 lesson); the DQB can be continued in a short follow-on slot if needed
LESSONS.aresKeywords: raw data, data collection, evidence, prediction, claim, categorical data, frequency (introduced informally), Driving Question Board

slo.purpose: To launch the anchoring phenomenon: Mr Otieno, the principal of Lakeview Senior School in Kisumu, has money for only one of three options (a school bus route, a bicycle shed or a second lunch serving), and learners give conflicting claims about how they travel to school. Learners predict the travel split, collect the 40 responses from Grade 10 Green and discover that an unorganised list cannot settle the argument. This creates the need to organise, summarise and display data.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (1) state that raw data is an unorganised list of responses; (2) explain why a claim such as 'almost everyone walks' needs evidence; (3) identify the six travel categories used by Grade 10 Green: Walk, Matatu, Boda boda, Bicycle, Private car, School bus; (4) explain why a long raw list is hard to use to decide between claims. Specific learning outcome link (KICD 3.1): collect data from the locality, such as means of transport used by learners to school; appreciate the importance of data organisation and interpretation in making effective decisions.
slo.skills: Making and recording a prediction with a reason (NGSS-style SEP: asking questions and defining problems; analysing and interpreting data). Collecting data accurately by recording one response per learner. Comparing a prediction with evidence. Asking testable questions. Communication and collaboration in pairs and groups. Core competencies: critical thinking and problem solving (interpretation and inference skills when collecting data); digital literacy is introduced later. PCI: Life Skills (Decision Making), shown when learners recognise that the principal needs evidence for an informed decision.
slo.attitudes: Integrity: learners record their own travel mode honestly and record others' responses accurately, even when it does not support their own claim. Love: learners are considerate of others' views when disagreeing about claims. Curiosity and openness to changing a prediction when evidence arrives.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we use statistics in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 is the anchoring lesson. It builds only on prior Grade 9 knowledge of collecting data. Learners leave with an unsettled argument, a raw list of 40 responses, an open Driving Question Board and a first draft model. The totals are NOT revealed in this lesson. Lesson 2 will organise the same raw list into a tally and frequency table.
slo.safetyNotes: No hazards. Handle the raw list sensitively: all names in the scenario are fictional, and learners may skip naming their own household transport details if uncomfortable (they only give one main travel mode). Avoid teasing about how anyone travels (for example private car versus walking). Remind learners that walking and cycling routes should be used safely and that no one should be ranked by how they travel. If learners have no devices, all tasks work on paper or the board.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Kamau opens by telling the class that Mr Otieno, the principal of Lakeview Senior School in Kisumu, has money for only one option: a school bus route, a bicycle shed or a second lunch serving. Three learners disagree: Atieno says 'Almost everyone walks', Brian says 'Most of us come by matatu', and Zawadi says 'The bus is always full'. Learners first write a private prediction of how Grade 10 Green (40 learners) travels to school and compare predictions in pairs. They then collect the real data: each learner gives ONE main way of travelling (Walk, Matatu, Boda boda, Bicycle, Private car, School bus) and the 40 responses are recorded in learner order 1 to 40 on the board or on a shared sheet, producing a long, confusing raw list: 1 W, 2 M, 3 W, 4 S, 5 M, 6 W, 7 B, 8 W, 9 M, 10 C, and so on to learner 40. Learners try to settle the claims from the list alone and discover how hard this is: nobody can say quickly who is right, and the list does not give a clear picture. They record what they notice and wonder, launch the Driving Question Board with the driving question 'How can we turn a messy list of data from our school into clear evidence that helps our principal make a fair decision?', sort questions into groups, and sketch a first draft model of how raw data might become evidence. No totals, percentages or graphs are shown; these are developed in later lessons.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners hear the principal's problem from Mr Kamau: Mr Otieno has money for only one of three choices (a school bus route, a bicycle shed or a second lunch serving). Learners read the three claims on the board: Atieno, 'Almost everyone walks'; Brian, 'Most of us come by matatu'; Zawadi, 'The bus is always full'. Individually, in their exercise books, they write: (a) which claim they think is closest to the truth for Grade 10 Green and why; (b) their own prediction of how many of the 40 learners use each mode: Walk, Matatu, Boda boda, Bicycle, Private car, School bus (the six numbers should add to 40); (c) which of the three options they think the principal should choose, and what evidence they would want. They then compare predictions with a partner and notice that predictions differ. Learners are not told the real totals.
framework.teacherMoves: Read the scenario aloud slowly, then say: 'Mr Otieno cannot buy everything. He can fund ONE thing. What would you want to know before you advise him?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before taking any answer. Display the three claims on the board without saying which is correct. Say: 'Write your prediction silently for 3 minutes. There is no wrong prediction today; it is your starting idea.' Circulate and look for learners who write numbers that do not add to 40; prompt with 'How many learners are there in total in our class?' Then pair learners for 2 minutes and cold-call 4 pairs (not volunteers) to share ONE number they disagreed on. Record 3 to 4 predicted Walk numbers on the board (for example 10, 20, 25, 30) without comment, and ask: 'Why do we not agree if we are all in the same class?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds. Do not reveal or hint at the actual counts.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: Prediction with reasoning (commit-before-evidence) plus Think-Pair-Share. Writing a private prediction first makes every learner hold a stake in the question, so the later raw list matters to them. Seeing different predictions side by side on the board shows that opinions alone cannot settle the argument, which creates the need for evidence. This links directly to the anchoring phenomenon: different learners, conflicting claims, one principal.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) each learner writes a prediction with a reason, not only a guess; (2) predictions for the six modes add to 40, or the learner corrects them after prompting; (3) at least 3 pairs name a type of evidence they would need, such as 'count everyone' or 'ask each learner'; (4) learners use the six mode names correctly. Quick check by show of hands: 'Who changed their mind after hearing a partner?' Note learners who rely only on feelings ('I just think') for follow-up in the later phases.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners collect the real data. Each learner answers ONE question: 'What is your main way of travelling to school?' choosing from Walk, Matatu, Boda boda, Bicycle, Private car, School bus. Responses are recorded in learner order 1 to 40 on a shared class sheet or the board, in the order of the register. The raw list reads: 1 W, 2 M, 3 W, 4 S, 5 M, 6 W, 7 B, 8 W, 9 M, 10 C, 11 W, 12 M, 13 Bi, 14 W, 15 M, 16 W, 17 S, 18 M, 19 W, 20 B, 21 M, 22 W, 23 C, 24 W, 25 M, 26 S, 27 W, 28 Bi, 29 M, 30 W, 31 B, 32 M, 33 W, 34 C, 35 S, 36 M, 37 W, 38 Bi, 39 B, 40 M. In pairs, learners copy the list and try to answer: (a) Is Atieno right that almost everyone walks? (b) Is Brian right that most of us come by matatu? (c) Does the list tell us whether the school needs a bus route, a bicycle shed or a second lunch serving? They record what they notice and what makes it hard (for example, they have to scan 40 items, they lose count, answers are in no order).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'We are now collecting evidence the way a real researcher would. Each person gives ONE main way of travelling, the way you travel MOST days.' Stress integrity: 'Record what is true, not what makes your claim win.' Call learners 1 to 40 in register order and write each response in the order given, using the codes W, M, B, Bi, C, S. Have a learner scribe check each entry aloud. Once the list is complete, say: 'You have 4 minutes with your partner. Use only this list. Decide whether Atieno or Brian is right, and tell me how sure you are.' Do not teach tallying or tables; if a learner starts tallying, say: 'Interesting, hold that thought; first tell me how easy or hard it is.' Circulate and note who tallies, who loses count, and who gives up. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after asking 'How sure are you?' Cold-call 5 learners to give a verdict and one reason. Then ask: 'Can you tell Mr Otieno, in one sentence, who is right?' Let the silence stand. Do NOT reveal the totals or the answer.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: Evidence collection with a 'noticing and wondering' routine. Learners collect real data about themselves, so the evidence feels authentic. Working from the raw list forces them to meet the problem directly: the data exists but is not usable. Naming the difficulty ('it is long', 'I lost count', 'no order') builds the need for organisation and shows that data alone is not evidence until it is organised. This links to the phenomenon: the same list that seems meaningless can become decisive once organised.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) learners record their own response honestly and accurately; (2) the class list has exactly 40 entries with codes matching the six modes; (3) learners can describe the difficulty in their own words (for example 'too long to count by eye'); (4) at least 4 learners state that they cannot be sure which claim is right; (5) learners who begin to group or tally by themselves are noted for Lesson 2 but not stopped. Check notebooks for a copied list with no mistakes in order.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners discuss in groups of 4 what they can and cannot say from the raw list. They return to their predictions and the three claims. They decide for each claim whether the list lets them judge it: Atieno ('Almost everyone walks'), Brian ('Most of us come by matatu'), Zawadi ('The bus is always full'). They discuss whether the class data can speak about Zawadi's claim at all (the school has a single 14-seater bus serving the whole school, but this class list is only Grade 10 Green, so it gives limited information about that claim). They write a short statement: 'The raw list helps us by ___, but it does not help us because ___.' They also say what the principal would want before choosing one of the three options, and why one class may not be enough to speak for the whole school.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Turn to your group. Take 4 minutes. For each claim, can the list prove it, disprove it, or can we not tell? Give a reason.' Circulate and ask: 'What would you need to do to the list to be sure?' Press for reasoning: 'You said it looks like many walk. What does "many" mean to Mr Otieno?' Probe Zawadi's claim: 'Zawadi says the bus is always full. Which part of our list could confirm that?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 groups. Introduce the key ideas in plain words only: 'raw data is the unorganised list; a claim needs evidence; one class is a small group compared with the whole school.' Do not give totals, frequency tables, percentages, or mean, median or mode (these belong to later lessons). Close with: 'So we have data but no decision. What is missing?' Collect 4 to 5 responses on the board under the heading 'What we need'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) discussion in groups. Learners judge each claim against the data, state what the evidence can and cannot support, and give a reason. This builds the habit of separating opinion from evidence, which is the core idea behind the driving question. Distinguishing what the class data can say from what it cannot (for example the bus claim, or the whole school) develops careful reasoning about sample size without using technical terms. It connects to the phenomenon because conflicting claims remain unresolved by the raw list.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) groups give reasons using the list rather than feelings; (2) at least 3 groups say 'we cannot tell' for at least one claim and explain why; (3) learners use the term 'evidence' correctly; (4) at least 2 groups notice that one class is not the whole school; (5) learners can state what is missing (a clearer organised summary). Use a quick thumbs-up/down check: 'Can the raw list alone settle Atieno and Brian's argument?' Expect most thumbs down. Follow up with learners whose thumbs are up, asking them to show how they know.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners help launch the Driving Question Board. The driving question is posted at the top: 'How can we turn a messy list of data from our school into clear evidence that helps our principal make a fair decision?' Each learner writes 2 questions on sticky notes or paper strips from what they have seen (for example 'How many of us walk?', 'How can we count quickly without mistakes?', 'Is one class enough?', 'Is it fair to decide on the bus from this?', 'What is the best way to show the results?'). In groups, they cluster similar questions and agree on 3 to 4 category headings. The class posts a key inquiry link: 'How do we use statistics in day-to-day life?' Learners also add the three claims (Atieno, Brian, Zawadi) and the raw list to the board as the starting evidence.
framework.teacherMoves: Post the driving question and read it aloud. Say: 'This is our big question for the next lessons. Write 2 questions of your own that you want answered. They can be small or big.' Give 3 minutes of silent writing. Then say: 'Bring your notes up and stick them where they belong. If a question looks like another one, put them together.' Cold-call 5 learners to read one question aloud and say why it matters. Help the class form clusters such as 'Counting and organising', 'Summaries and averages', 'Graphs and pictures', 'Fairness and trust' and 'Whole school'. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before asking: 'Which questions do you think we can answer first?' Mark with a star the questions about counting and organising. Say: 'We will return to this board at the end of every lesson.' Do not answer the questions now; note the ones on mean, median and mode to revisit later.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: Driving Question Board with question clustering. Learners turn their confusion into questions they own, and clustering shows patterns in what the class wants to know. The board becomes a visible record of understanding that grows from lesson to lesson, so learners can see their questions being answered. It connects to the phenomenon because every question traces back to the unresolved problem of how to turn the messy list into a fair decision for Mr Otieno.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) each learner posts at least 2 questions; (2) at least half the questions are about organising, summarising or showing data rather than yes/no or off-topic questions; (3) learners can justify the cluster headings; (4) at least 3 learners ask about fairness or whether the data is enough (for example one class versus the whole school); (5) learners connect questions to the principal's decision. Note learners who write only 'what is statistics?' for gentle follow-up. Photograph or keep the board for use in later lessons.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners draw a first draft model in their books to show their current thinking about how a messy list of data could become evidence for the principal. The model includes: (1) the messy raw list of 40 responses; (2) a box or arrow labelled with their idea of what should happen next (for example 'count', 'sort', 'draw something'); (3) the output they expect (a clear answer for Mr Otieno); (4) a question mark where they are unsure. They add a short caption: 'What I think will make the data useful is ___.' Pairs swap models and give one comment each. Learners also complete the first column of a summary table: 'What we observed' (a 40-response list, conflicting claims, no clear answer).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Draw how you think a messy list could turn into clear evidence for Mr Otieno. Use boxes and arrows. It is fine if you are unsure; put a question mark where you do not know.' Model with a quick sketch of two boxes and one arrow without filling in the steps. Circulate and ask: 'What happens to the 40 responses in your model?' and 'How will you know your answer is right?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Ask pairs to swap and say one thing they like and one question they have. Cold-call 3 learners to share their 'what I think will make it useful' caption. Do not correct the models; say: 'We will revise these models at the end of the next lessons.' Collect the models or tell learners to keep them safely in their books. Remind learners that tomorrow they will start organising the same list.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: Initial model drawing (cumulative model building). Drawing a first draft makes learners' ideas visible, including gaps and misconceptions, and gives a baseline to compare with later. Because the model will be revised after each lesson, learners see how their understanding develops from raw list to organised table, summaries and graphs. It links to the phenomenon as the model explains how a messy list could become a decisive piece of evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) the model shows the raw list leading to some organised or summarised output; (2) learners include at least one action (count, sort, group, draw); (3) learners mark uncertainty with a question mark or note; (4) the caption refers to evidence for the principal; (5) peer comments are specific. Use a quick exit prompt: 'In one sentence, why can we not decide from the raw list alone?' Check that at least most learners write about the list being long, unorganised or hard to count.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Did learners commit to a prediction before seeing the data, and did the differing predictions create real curiosity? Did the raw list feel genuinely confusing, so learners saw the need for organisation, or did some learners quickly tally it and settle the argument? If so, how will you build on this in Lesson 2? Which learners relied on opinion rather than evidence? Were all learners comfortable giving their travel mode honestly, with no teasing? Did learners notice the limits of one class and the point that the bus claim cannot be judged from this class list? Which questions on the DQB are most useful for Lesson 2 (tally and frequency tables)? Keep the board, the raw list and the draft models for revisiting in later lessons. Did you avoid revealing the totals?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What did we observe? We collected 40 responses from Grade 10 Green about main travel mode (Walk, Matatu, Boda boda, Bicycle, Private car, School bus), saw three conflicting claims from Atieno, Brian and Zawadi, and found the long raw list was hard to use to say who is right.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What did we learn? Raw data is an unorganised list; a claim needs evidence; a long list does not settle an argument by itself, and one class is not the whole school.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: How can we explain it so far? We have data but not yet evidence for Mr Otieno because the list is unorganised. We predict that organising and showing the data will make the answer clearer, but we still need to find out how, and which summary or graph to trust.

LESSONS.title: Tally and Frequency Tables: Making Sense of the 40 Responses
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one lesson; the 5 phases are done in sequence, with a short extension for the DQB and model)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: raw data, tally marks, frequency, frequency table, categorical data, discrete data, total frequency, percentage, evidence, Kisumu, travel to school

slo.purpose: Learners organise the raw list of 40 travel responses into a tally and frequency table, check that the frequencies add to the total of 40, and judge how far the table helps settle the claims about how the class travels to school.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (a) define raw data, tally marks and frequency; (b) draw a frequency distribution table (Category, Tally, Frequency) for ungrouped categorical and discrete data; (c) check that the frequencies add up to the total number of responses; (d) calculate the percentage for each category using f / n x 100.
slo.skills: Collecting and organising data, tallying in groups of five, checking totals, reading a table to extract information, comparing two representations of the same data (raw list and table), and communicating a conclusion using evidence. NGSS Science and Engineering Practices embedded: Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking; Constructing Explanations.
slo.attitudes: Integrity: honesty while working in groups and making frequency tables (no adjusting counts to fit a favourite claim). Love: consideration of others when working with peers to extract information and draw conclusions. Appreciate the importance of data organisation and interpretation in making effective decisions. Core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving (interpretation and inference skills when collecting data). PCI: Life Skills (Decision Making).
slo.keyInquiry: How do we use statistics in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 left learners with a raw list of 40 responses from Grade 10 Green and three claims (Atieno: 'Almost everyone walks'; Brian: 'Most of us come by matatu'; Zawadi: 'The bus is always full') that the unorganised list could not settle. In this lesson learners build the frequency table (Walk 14, Matatu 12, Boda boda 4, Bicycle 3, Private car 3, School bus 4 = 40) and see for the first time that the same data becomes readable once organised. This gives the evidence base that Lessons 3 to 7 will summarise (mean, median, mode) and display (graphs and pie charts) before the Lesson 8 recommendation to Mr Otieno. The lesson does not yet teach mode, mean, median or graphs.
slo.safetyNotes: Low-risk classroom activity. Learners share the class list respectfully and never tease a classmate about how they travel (for example boda boda or walking long distances). Names are not attached to answers on the display; use learner numbers 1 to 40 only. Pencils and rulers are handled carefully, and learners keep walkways clear when moving to the board.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Kamau returns the raw list of 40 travel responses from Lesson 1 (learner numbers 1 to 40, coded W, M, B, Bi, C, S). Learners first predict what a more organised version might show, then work in groups of four to tally the 40 responses into five-bar-gate tally marks, count frequencies and check that they add to 40. They compare the raw list with the table and test the claims of Atieno, Brian and Zawadi against the evidence. Walk 14 and Matatu 12 are the largest groups, neither is more than half, and together they make 26 of 40, which is 65%. Learners then apply the same skill to a new data set (30 trees in the Lakeview compound: Grevillea 12, Cypress 8, Eucalyptus 6, Neem 4) and discuss discrete data. They add new questions to the Driving Question Board and revise their first draft model: raw data must be organised before it can be used as evidence. Zawadi's claim about the bus cannot be tested with this class table because the school has one 14-seater bus serving the whole school, which is a question for the DQB.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the raw list from Lesson 1 displayed on the board (1 W, 2 M, 3 W, 4 S ... 40 M). Individually, then in pairs, they write a prediction in their books: 'If we count how many learners use each way of travelling, which way will have the most learners, and about how many? Will anyone be right: Atieno, Brian or Zawadi?' They also predict: 'What would we have to do to the list to see the answer quickly?' Pairs share their predicted counts for Walk and Matatu, and write them in a prediction column to be checked later.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the raw list in learner order. Say: 'Yesterday we could not settle Atieno's and Brian's argument from this list. Before we do any counting, write down your best prediction: which mode of travel will have the most learners, and how many?' Give 1 minute silent writing, then WAIT TIME of 10 seconds after asking: 'What could we do to this list to make it easier to read?' Cold-call 3 learners for their predicted counts and 2 learners for ideas on organising (listen for 'count', 'group', 'table'). Record predictions on the board in a Prediction column without judging. Say: 'We will check these predictions with evidence before the lesson ends.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with commitment (Predict-Observe-Explain): learners put a numerical prediction on record, so that comparing it with the actual frequency table creates cognitive conflict or confirmation. Naming the need to organise the list helps learners see why a table is needed, and links back to Lesson 1's unsettled claims.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether learners write a specific numerical prediction rather than just a category. Look for: (1) predictions that name a category and an approximate count; (2) learners who connect to a claim (Atieno, Brian or Zawadi); (3) ideas about counting or grouping. Note the 3 or 4 learners who predict that nobody can know without counting; they have the right idea for the Observe phase.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of four, learners receive a copy of the raw list (learner numbers 1 to 40 with codes W, M, B, Bi, C, S). Step 1: draw a table with three columns: Category, Tally, Frequency, and six rows in the order Walk, Matatu, Boda boda, Bicycle, Private car, School bus. Step 2: one learner reads the list aloud, response by response, while another puts a tally mark in the correct row, grouping every five marks (four strokes crossed by a fifth). Step 3: each group counts tallies to fill the Frequency column, then adds the six frequencies to see whether they equal 40. Step 4: groups whose total is not 40 find the mistake (a missed or double-counted response) by re-reading the list. The final agreed table is Walk 14, Matatu 12, Boda boda 4, Bicycle 3, Private car 3, School bus 4 = 40. Step 5: groups add a Percentage column using f / n x 100: Walk 35%, Matatu 30%, Boda boda 10%, Bicycle 7.5%, Private car 7.5%, School bus 10% (sum 100%). Learners compare the table to the raw list and record two things the table shows that the list did not.
framework.teacherMoves: Model the first 5 responses on the board: 'Learner 1 is W, so I put one stroke in the Walk row. Learner 2 is M, one stroke in Matatu.' Show how the fifth stroke crosses the four. Circulate and ask: 'How do you know you have not missed learner 23?' and 'What should the six frequencies add up to? Why?' Insist on one reader and one tally keeper, switching roles halfway so every learner does both. If a group's total is not 40, do not give the error; say 'Your total is 39. Where could a response have gone missing? Re-read together.' Give groups a WAIT TIME of 10 to 15 seconds before offering a hint. After 10 minutes, ask 4 groups (cold-call by group number) to read their frequencies; write them on the board and resolve any disagreement by tallying the disputed rows together. Remind learners to be honest and report what the list really says, even if it contradicts their own prediction (Integrity). Remind them to use learner numbers, not names.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data organisation as evidence-building: learners physically transform an unorganised list into a table and use the total check (frequencies must add to 40) as a built-in error detector. The side-by-side comparison of the raw list with the table builds understanding that organisation, not new data, creates the clarity.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) tally marks are grouped in fives correctly; (2) the six rows appear in the order Walk, Matatu, Boda boda, Bicycle, Private car, School bus; (3) frequencies are 14, 12, 4, 3, 3, 4; (4) the group checks that they sum to 40 without being prompted; (5) percentages are computed as f / 40 x 100. Use a quick checklist per group. Common errors to watch for: counting the learner number instead of the response; ending with a total of 39 or 41; tallying with five single strokes instead of a gate; forgetting that Bicycle (Bi) and Boda boda (B) are different rows.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use the completed table to test the three claims. In pairs they answer: (a) Is Atieno right that 'almost everyone walks'? Use the number and percentage. (b) Is Brian right that 'most of us come by matatu'? (c) Can the table settle Zawadi's claim that 'the bus is always full'? Learners find that 14 of 40 (35%) walk, which is the largest group but not almost everyone; 12 of 40 (30%) use a matatu, so not most; walk and matatu together are 26 of 40, 65%. For the bus, only 4 of 40 learners in Grade 10 Green use it, but Zawadi's claim is about the school's single 14-seater bus serving the whole school, so this class table cannot confirm or refute it. Learners then practise on new data: the 30 trees in the Lakeview compound (raw list given: for example G, C, G, E, N ...) and complete a tally and frequency table to get Grevillea 12, Cypress 8, Eucalyptus 6, Neem 4 = 30. They write one sentence in the form 'The most common tree is ___ with ___ out of ___.' and decide how the tree data differs from travel data. Discussion on discrete data: counts such as number of siblings are numbers, while travel mode and tree type are categories; both can go into the same Category/Value, Tally, Frequency layout. Finally, learners revisit their predictions and mark whether each was close.
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: 'Using only the table, is Atieno right that almost everyone walks? Give me a number.' Give WAIT TIME of 10 to 15 seconds, then cold-call 3 pairs for each claim. Press for evidence: 'What does 14 out of 40 tell you? Is that more than half? How do you know?' For Zawadi: 'Our table says 4 learners use the bus. Does that prove the bus is not full?' Wait 10 seconds. Guide to: the bus is a single 14-seater serving the whole school, so one class cannot confirm or refute it; we would need data from the whole school. Do not tell learners the answer to the whole-school question. For the tree practice, supply the raw list of 30 responses and let pairs work independently for 6 minutes; cold-call 2 pairs to read their frequencies, and have the class check that the total is 30. Ask: 'How is travel mode different from number of siblings? Which one is a count?' Introduce the terms categorical and discrete data clearly and briefly, and say 'We are not yet finding the mean, median or mode; that comes next lesson.' Praise precise evidence-based sentences: 'Good, you used the number 14 out of 40 to support your claim.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER): learners state a claim about each learner's statement, cite specific frequencies and percentages as evidence, and give reasoning (for example 'more than half would be more than 20 learners'). Transferring the same skill to the tree data checks understanding of the table-building procedure in a new context, and the categorical versus discrete contrast develops understanding of data types.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for CER statements that cite numbers (14 of 40, 12 of 40, 26 of 40, 65%) and use 'more than half' reasoning (more than 20). Check that learners do not claim the table proves anything about the school bus being full. Collect the tree tables: correct frequencies are 12, 8, 6, 4 summing to 30. Exit-ticket style check on whiteboards: 'Write the frequency and percentage for Matatu.' Expected: 12 and 30%. Note learners who still confuse frequency with percentage for re-teaching in small groups.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board started in Lesson 1, which displays: 'How can we turn a messy list of data from our school into clear evidence that helps our principal make a fair decision?' Each learner writes one new question or one new answer on a sticky note or paper slip. Examples: 'Is one class enough to decide for the whole school?' 'How can we show the table as a picture?' 'Which number best represents how we travel?' 'How full is the school bus if only 4 of us use it?' Learners place notes on the board and, as a class, sort them into groups: ones answered by the table (for example how many walk), ones to be answered in later lessons (summaries and graphs), and ones that need more data (the whole school and the bus). Learners mark a note answered: 'Which mode of travel is most common in our class? Walk, 14.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Put one thing we can now answer and one new question on the board. Use learner numbers, not names, if you mention classmates.' Give 1 minute of silent thinking and WAIT TIME of 10 seconds before they write. Cold-call 4 learners to read and place their notes and say why. Ask: 'Which of these questions can the table already answer? Which need something more than a table?' Move the answered notes to an 'Answered by evidence' column and label two columns: 'Need a typical value or graph' and 'Need whole-school data'. Point out that Zawadi's bus claim sits in the last column. Preview: 'Next lesson we will find one typical value for our data.' Do not answer future questions now.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question sorting on the DQB: learners categorise questions by the type of evidence needed. This tracks growing understanding and builds a visible link between what has been learned (frequency table), what is still unknown (typical value, graphs, whole school) and the final recommendation for Mr Otieno.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check whether each learner posts a relevant question or answered statement and whether they place it in a sensible group. Look for questions that show awareness that one class is a small sample, or that the table needs a picture. Note learners whose questions are only 'what is a tally?' and who need support. Record 3 strong questions to guide planning for Lesson 3.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the first draft model from Lesson 1 (a diagram or flow chart showing how data goes from collection to a decision for the principal). Individually or in pairs, they add a new step between 'collect raw data' and 'decide': 'Organise into a tally and frequency table, then check the frequencies add up to the total.' They add an example box: 'Travel: Walk 14, Matatu 12, Boda boda 4, Bicycle 3, Private car 3, School bus 4 = 40.' They also write a limits note: 'One class (Grade 10 Green) is a small sample; the table alone does not choose between a bus, a shed or a second lunch serving.' Learners compare their updated models with a neighbour and fix any missing steps. Optionally they complete the sentence: 'The same list looks meaningless as raw data but clear as a table because ___.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your model from Lesson 1. What step is missing between collecting the 40 responses and advising Mr Otieno? Add it now with the numbers.' Give 2 minutes of silent work, then WAIT TIME of 10 seconds before asking: 'What did you add and why?' Cold-call 3 learners to explain their new step. Ask a probing question: 'Does the table tell Mr Otieno what to build?' Guide learners to the limits: it shows which groups are bigger, but they still need typical values and graphs and data from the whole school. Collect a photo or note of 3 models to plan the next lesson. Close with: 'Next lesson we will find a typical value for our data.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: learners add a new mechanism (organising data into a frequency table with a total check) to their evolving model of how raw data becomes evidence. Writing a limits note supports scientific reasoning about uncertainty and sample size.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) the new step is placed between collecting and deciding; (2) it mentions tally, frequency and the total check; (3) the example uses correct travel numbers (14, 12, 4, 3, 3, 4 = 40); (4) a limits note on sample size. Use a 3-level quick check: step present but no numbers; step with numbers; step with numbers and limits note. Plan a short re-teach for learners at the first level.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) Did every group get a total of 40 on its own, and which strategies did they use to find a missing or double-counted response? (2) Which learners still mix up frequency and percentage, or tally with five single strokes instead of the gate? (3) Did learners avoid claiming that the table proves anything about the school bus, and recognise that one class is a small sample? (4) Did the comparison between the raw list and the table help learners see why organisation matters? (5) Were the learners' predictions close to 14 and 12, and how did they react to the evidence? Note which DQB questions to carry into Lesson 3 (typical value: mode and mean) and which learners need support with the Category, Tally, Frequency layout. Ensure learner names stay out of the displayed data.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We tallied the 40 raw responses from Grade 10 Green and got Walk 14, Matatu 12, Boda boda 4, Bicycle 3, Private car 3, School bus 4, which add to 40. Percentages are Walk 35%, Matatu 30%, Boda boda 10%, Bicycle 7.5%, Private car 7.5%, School bus 10%. For the 30 trees in the Lakeview compound we got Grevillea 12, Cypress 8, Eucalyptus 6, Neem 4.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: A frequency table has the columns Category (or Value), Tally and Frequency. Tally marks are grouped in fives, and the frequencies must add up to the total number of responses. Percentage = f / n x 100. Categorical data (travel mode, tree type) and discrete data (counts such as siblings) can both be organised this way.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The raw list could not settle the argument, but the table shows Walk (14 of 40, 35%) is the largest group and Matatu (12 of 40, 30%) is second. Neither is more than half, so 'almost everyone walks' and 'most come by matatu' are both wrong, although together they make 26 of 40, which is 65%. Only 4 of 40 use the school bus and 3 of 40 cycle. The table cannot settle Zawadi's claim about the single 14-seater school bus, and one class is a small sample, so we need typical values, graphs and whole-school data before advising Mr Otieno.

LESSONS.title: Typical Value: Mode and Mean
LESSONS.aresKeywords: mode, mean, frequency table, Σfx, Σf, typical value, ungrouped data, siblings, Walk

slo.purpose: Learners find the mode from a frequency table and calculate the mean using Σfx ÷ Σf for ungrouped data, so they can describe a 'typical' value in Grade 10 Green's data for Mr Otieno.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) determine the mode of ungrouped data from a frequency table (the value or category with the highest frequency); (b) calculate the mean of ungrouped data using Σfx ÷ Σf from a frequency table with an fx column; (c) explain why the mode can be used for categories (travel mode = Walk, 14) while the mean applies only to numbers (siblings: mean 83 ÷ 40 = 2.075, about 2.1 siblings; mode 2).
slo.skills: Reading and extending a frequency table (adding an fx column); multiplying and adding systematically; checking that Σf equals the total of 40; rounding to 1 decimal place and giving units (siblings); constructing a written explanation of what 'typical' means. NGSS-aligned practices: Analysing and interpreting data; Using mathematics and computational thinking; Constructing explanations.
slo.attitudes: Integrity: the learner records and calculates honestly and checks results with peers. Love: the learner is considerate when partners make errors and helps them correct these. Appreciation of how summarising data helps in making effective decisions. Core competency: Critical thinking and problem solving (interpretation and inference). PCI: Life Skills (Decision Making).
slo.keyInquiry: How do we use statistics in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 showed that the raw list of 40 travel responses could not settle the claims. Lesson 2 organised the data into a frequency table (Walk 14; Matatu 12; Boda boda 4; Bicycle 3; Private car 3; School bus 4). Lesson 3 asks 'what is typical for our class?' Learners find the mode of travel (Walk) and the mode and mean of a numerical set (siblings of the same 40 learners). They see that one number can summarise a table, but that the mean fits only numbers. Lesson 4 will add the median and ask which measure is best.
slo.safetyNotes: No hazards. Calculators are optional and should be shared fairly. Siblings data is sensitive: families differ, so learners give only a number, no names or comments about family size, and respect for classmates is stressed.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Otieno asks, 'What is the typical Grade 10 Green learner at Lakeview Senior School in Kisumu?' Learners first predict a typical travel mode and a typical number of siblings. They then use the frequency table from Lesson 2 to find the mode of travel (Walk, 14 of 40). Next they work with the siblings table (0 siblings 5; 1 sibling 9; 2 siblings 12; 3 siblings 8; 4 siblings 4; 5 siblings 2; total 40), find the mode (2) and build an fx column to calculate the mean (0+9+24+24+16+10 = 83; 83 ÷ 40 = 2.075, about 2.1 siblings). They discuss why a mean of 2.1 siblings is not a real family, why the mean cannot be found for travel mode, and what these summaries do and do not tell the principal. The median and the choice of best measure are left for Lesson 4.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 7 minutes) Learners are reminded of the principal's problem and of Lesson 2's frequency table. Individually, on scrap paper, they write: (1) the 'typical' way a Grade 10 Green learner travels to school; (2) their prediction of the 'typical' number of siblings a learner in the class has, and why. They are told the class's siblings counts were recorded as a frequency table. They pair up and compare, then 3-4 pairs share predictions. Learners can see that some predicted a whole number and some a decimal.
framework.teacherMoves: Write on the board: 'Mr Otieno asks: what is a TYPICAL Grade 10 Green learner?' Say: 'Without calculating, write down the typical way we travel to school and the typical number of siblings. You have 2 minutes of silent thinking.' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after asking, 'What does the word typical mean to you?' before taking answers. Cold-call 4 learners (not volunteers) for their sibling prediction and record all predictions as tally marks on the board. Ask: 'Who thinks typical means the most common? Who thinks it means the middle or fair share?' Do not correct yet. Say: 'Keep your prediction. We will test it with the data.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with a public record (Think-Pair-Share). Writing a prediction first, then comparing, makes learners commit to an idea and notice that 'typical' can mean different things, which creates the need for precise measures (mode and mean).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe: Do learners give reasons, not just guesses? Do at least 3 different meanings of 'typical' (most common, middle, share) come out? Note learners who predict travel mode 'Walk' or 'Matatu' using Lesson 2's table. Look for the prediction that 'typical' is a fair share, a hint of the mean. Record the class range of sibling predictions on the board for later comparison.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 13 minutes) Part A (4 min): From the Lesson 2 travel table, learners underline the highest frequency and find the mode: Walk (14). They check that the frequencies add to 40. Part B (9 min): In pairs, they receive the siblings frequency table (0 siblings 5; 1 sibling 9; 2 siblings 12; 3 siblings 8; 4 siblings 4; 5 siblings 2). They (1) check Σf = 40, (2) find the mode (2 siblings, f = 12), (3) add a third column fx (value x frequency): 0, 9, 24, 24, 16, 10, (4) add the fx column to get Σfx = 83, (5) divide 83 ÷ 40 = 2.075, about 2.1 siblings. They compare the result with their prediction.
framework.teacherMoves: Part A: 'Look at last lesson's travel table. Which group has the highest frequency? Show me with your finger.' WAIT TIME 10 seconds. Cold-call 2 learners: 'What is the mode of travel? How do you know?' Write: 'Mode = value or category with the highest frequency.' Part B: Say: 'The mode tells us which is most common. To share all the siblings out fairly, we need the mean. Add a new column called fx.' Model ONE row on the board: '3 siblings x 8 learners = 24 siblings. Why multiply?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Circulate with the prompt: 'Where is your check that the f column adds to 40?' Watch for learners who add the x values (0+1+2+3+4+5 = 15) or divide by 6 rows instead of 40; ask, 'How many learners are there altogether? So what do we divide by?' Ensure answers are rounded to 1 d.p. with units. Write: 'Mean = Σfx ÷ Σf'. Use the word 'mean', never 'average'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured table construction (extending the frequency table with an fx column) and Notice and Wonder. The fx column makes the repeated-addition idea visible, so learners see why the mean needs frequencies, linking to Lesson 2's f column. Contrasting the mode (a count) with the mean (a share) shows two meanings of 'typical'.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check observable indicators: (1) Σf = 40 is checked before calculating; (2) fx values are 0, 9, 24, 24, 16, 10; (3) Σfx = 83; (4) the divisor is 40, not 6; (5) the mean is written as 2.1 siblings; (6) the mode of siblings is given as 2, not 12. Tally how many pairs reach 83. Pairs who get a different Σfx must find their own error by checking each row. Note common errors: giving the mode as the frequency (12), or ignoring the 0 siblings row.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 10 minutes) Learners work in groups of 4 to answer: (1) The mean is 2.1 siblings, but no learner has 2.1 siblings. What does 2.1 mean? (2) The mode of travel is Walk; why can we not calculate a mean of travel mode? (3) Mode 2 and mean 2.1 for siblings are close; Walk is the mode of travel, but it is only 14 of 40. Does 'Almost everyone walks' hold? (4) Mini-problem: Mama Achieng's mandazi sold on 5 days are 40, 45, 42, 50 and 45. Find the mean (222 ÷ 5 = 44.4 mandazi) and the mode (45). Each group writes a claim-evidence-reasoning statement for Mr Otieno: 'The typical Grade 10 Green learner ... because ...'.
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: 'Nobody has 2.1 siblings. Is the mean wrong? Talk in your groups.' WAIT TIME 15 seconds before sharing. Cold-call 3 groups (not volunteers). Use the revoicing prompt: 'Who can say that again in different words?' Guide: 'Imagine all 83 siblings shared out equally among 40 learners: how many each?' Push the link to the phenomenon: 'Walk is the mode with 14. Is 14 out of 40 almost everyone? What fraction, as a percentage?' (35%, from the Lesson 2 table.) Say: 'Walk is the most common group, but 35% is not more than half. The mode names the biggest group; it does not say it is the majority.' Provide the sentence frame: 'The typical learner ... The evidence is ... This helps Mr Otieno because ...'. Note that the median, and which measure is best, come in Lesson 4: 'Hold that question for next lesson.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with group discussion. Learners must justify a claim using the mode and mean as evidence and reason about what each measure can and cannot show. Contrasting categorical and numerical data builds understanding of when each measure applies.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for explanations that (a) say the mean is a fair-share value that need not be a whole number; (b) say the mean needs numbers, so it cannot apply to Walk, Matatu and so on; (c) cite 14 of 40 (35%) to show that the mode is not a majority; (d) get 44.4 mandazi and 45 correctly. Use a 3-level check: Meets = correct calculations and one correct explanation; Exceeds = also explains the limits of both measures with data from the lesson; Approaching = calculations only. Note groups for follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 5 minutes) Learners return to the Driving Question Board started in Lesson 1. Each writes on a sticky note one NEW question or one answered question from today. Examples: 'Is the mean always a better summary than the mode?' 'What if one learner had 15 siblings?' 'Does the typical travel mode tell Mr Otieno what to build?' They place notes under the headings 'Answered' or 'New questions' and read 2-3 aloud.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Write one question about typical values that you still have. Place it on the board.' WAIT TIME 10 seconds before the sharing. Cold-call 3 learners to read their notes. Move the question 'Which questions can the mode and mean help answer for Mr Otieno?' to the 'Answered' side, and mark questions about unusually large values and about the middle value as 'Coming in Lesson 4'. Ask: 'Which of today's ideas helps us answer the driving question?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board tracking. A visible record of answered and new questions keeps the learning linked to the principal's decision and shows how each lesson adds to the evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that notes are linked to today's content (mode, mean, typical) and that at least some are genuine questions (e.g., about unusual values), not statements. Count notes that identify limits of the mean or mode. Notice learners who have no note and invite them to add one verbally.

framework.learnerExperience: (About 5 minutes) Learners open their draft model (the statistics cycle from Lesson 1: collect, organise, summarise, display, interpret) and add a 'Summarise' step with the new tools: Mode = most frequent value or category (works for categories and numbers); Mean = Σfx ÷ Σf (numbers only). They add the evidence: Mode of travel = Walk (14 of 40, 35%); siblings mode 2, mean 83 ÷ 40 = 2.1 siblings. They write one sentence on what these summaries still cannot tell Mr Otieno.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Add the new step to your model. Show where the f column fits and write the formula in your own words.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then circulate and ask: 'Why does your model need both mode and mean?' Cold-call 2 learners to read their 'cannot tell' sentence (e.g., 'Mode: Walk does not show that most walk; the class is only 40 learners from one class'). Remind them that one class is a small sample and that Lesson 4 will ask which measure is best.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision. Revising the class model after each lesson makes learners connect new skills (mode, mean) to the whole data cycle and the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that models include: (1) the mode defined correctly; (2) the mean formula Σfx ÷ Σf; (3) a note that the mean needs numbers; (4) travel and siblings evidence with exact numbers; (5) one stated limit. Use the exit ticket: 'Find the mean and mode of: x = 1, 2, 3 with f = 2, 5, 3.' Expected: Σf = 10; Σfx = 2+10+9 = 21; mean 2.1; mode 2.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners confused the mode (2 siblings) with its frequency (12), or divided Σfx by the number of rows (6) instead of Σf (40)? Did the idea that the mean is a fair share (83 siblings shared among 40 learners) make sense to learners? Were any learners uncomfortable about sibling counts, and was the respectful norm kept? Did learners notice that Walk is the mode but only 35%, so 'almost everyone walks' is not supported? Which learners need more practice with an fx column before the median is introduced in Lesson 4?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: The travel table has its highest frequency at Walk (14 of 40, 35%). The siblings table has its highest frequency at 2 siblings (12 of 40). Adding an fx column gives Σfx = 83 for Σf = 40.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The mode is the value or category with the highest frequency and works for categories and numbers. The mean = Σfx ÷ Σf and works only for numbers. Mean of siblings = 83 ÷ 40 = 2.075, about 2.1 siblings; mode = 2. Travel mode: Walk is the mode but is not a majority.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The typical Grade 10 Green learner walks to school and has about 2 siblings. The mean (2.1) need not be a whole number because it is a fair share. These summaries describe only this one class, so they are not enough alone to support a decision by Mr Otieno; we need to know when each measure is the best choice (Lesson 4).

LESSONS.title: Median and Choosing the Best Measure
LESSONS.aresKeywords: median, ordered data, middle value, mean, mode, outlier, best measure, siblings, runner times, evidence

slo.purpose: Learners find the median of ordered ungrouped data for odd and even n, including from a frequency table using cumulative counting, and decide whether mean, median or mode best represents a data set, including the effect of an outlier.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (a) determine the median of ungrouped data (SLO 3.1 b: determine mean, mode and median of ungrouped data); (b) explain when the mean, median or mode best represents a data set, including how one extreme value affects the mean; (c) appreciate the importance of data organisation and interpretation in making effective decisions (SLO 3.1 e). Median = the middle value of ordered data: for odd n it is the ((n+1)/2)th value; for even n it is the mean of the two middle values.
slo.skills: Ordering data, cumulative counting from a frequency table, locating the middle position, calculating to 1 decimal place with units, comparing measures, and justifying a choice with evidence (NGSS-style practices: analysing and interpreting data; engaging in argument from evidence).
slo.attitudes: Core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving (interpretation and inference when comparing measures). Values: Integrity (honest use of data, not removing a value just to get a nicer answer) and Love (considerate listening to peers' arguments). PCI: Life Skills (Decision Making), choosing the summary that gives a fair picture to decision-makers.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we use statistics in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 3 gave the class the mode and the mean (siblings mean 2.1, mode 2; mode of travel = Walk). Lesson 4 adds the median and shows that the three measures can agree (siblings) or disagree (runner times), so the best summary depends on the data type and the question. This prepares learners to display data in Lessons 5 to 7 and to give Mr Otieno an honest recommendation in Lesson 8. Note: mean and median do not apply to travel mode because it is categories, so only the mode summarises it.
slo.safetyNotes: Pen, paper and calculators only. Ensure learners do not tease peers about family size or about being slow runners. Use the fictional Eldoret club group and avoid naming real athletes or learners' real families; allow learners to opt out of sharing personal sibling data.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Kamau returns to Mr Otieno's problem: the class has a table of travel data and can summarise number data, but which single number should the principal trust? Learners first predict which of three measures best describes a set of runner times. They then find the median of the siblings data using cumulative frequencies (20th and 21st values, both 2, so the median is 2) and the median of the Eldoret club 800 m times (4th of 7 values = 106 s), compare these with the mean and mode (109.3 s and 105 s), and test what happens to the mean when the 130 s time is removed (105.8 s). In the Explain phase they build a rule for choosing a measure. The class updates the Driving Question Board and revises its model of how raw data becomes evidence.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall Lesson 3 (mode and mean). Mr Kamau writes the 7 Eldoret club 800 m times on the board in unordered form: 107, 130, 105, 104, 108, 105, 106 seconds. He tells learners the coach must tell a selector 'how fast this group is'. Individually, on paper, learners write: (1) a prediction of the 'typical' time, as a number, before any calculating; (2) which measure they think will describe the group best (mean, mode or something else) and why. They share with a partner for 2 minutes and then record agreements and disagreements. Learners also link back: 'In the travel data we could only use the mode. Will it be different for numbers?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'A selector in Eldoret asks the coach, how fast is this group? The coach must give ONE number. Write down the number you would give before we calculate anything.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds of silent thinking before any talk. Say: 'Now turn to your partner and compare. Do you agree?' Cold-call 4 pairs (not volunteers) to state their predicted number. Record all on the board without judging. Ask: 'Which of the measures we learned in Lesson 3, mean or mode, did you lean on, and why?' Do NOT mention the median yet. Circulate and note learners who pick the mean automatically.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with commitment (Predict-Observe-Explain): learners commit to a number and a reason in writing before instruction. This surfaces the preconception that the mean is always the best summary and creates a cognitive need for comparing measures, which later evidence will test.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that at least 80% of learners have written a numerical prediction AND a reason. Listen for: 'mean because it uses all the numbers' (common preconception) versus 'mode because most runners did 105'. Note the number of learners who predict between 104 and 110 s versus outside that range. Look for any learner who notices that 130 s looks unusual; record their name for use in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (siblings, same 40 learners): Learners use the siblings frequency table: 0 siblings 5; 1 sibling 9; 2 siblings 12; 3 siblings 8; 4 siblings 4; 5 siblings 2 (total 40). They add a cumulative frequency column: 5, 14, 26, 34, 38, 40. Since n = 40 is even, the median is the mean of the 20th and 21st values. In pairs they find both lie in the group with cumulative frequency reaching 26 (positions 15 to 26), so both values are 2 and the median is 2 siblings. They compare with the mean (83/40 = 2.1 siblings) and mode (2 siblings) from Lesson 3: all three agree. Part B (runner times): They order the 7 times: 104, 105, 105, 106, 107, 108, 130 s. n = 7 is odd, so the median is the (7+1)/2 = 4th value = 106 s. They find the mode, 105 s, and the mean, 765/7 = 109.3 s. They then remove 130 s and find the mean of the other six: 635/6 = 105.8 s. They record all results in an Observation Table: Data set | Mean | Median | Mode | Do they agree? Part C (even n practice): they find the median of the 6 times without 130 s: 104, 105, 105, 106, 107, 108, which gives the 3rd and 4th values 105 and 106, so the median is 105.5 s.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute printed tables or have learners draw them. Say: 'First, ORDER the data. A median from an unordered list is wrong. Why must we order first?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. For siblings say: 'There are 40 learners. Which positions are in the middle? Count with me, 20th and 21st. Use the cumulative column to find which group the 20th learner is in.' Cold-call 3 learners to say which group contains the 20th and which contains the 21st. For runners say: 'Seven values, odd number. Use (n+1)/2. What position?' Cold-call 2 learners. Circulate with a checklist: Did they order? Did they use the right position? Correct common errors: finding the median as the middle of the list of categories (0 to 5, giving 2.5) rather than the middle of the 40 values; forgetting to divide by 7 for the mean. Say: 'Check your mean is not equal to any of the actual times. What do you notice about 109.3 compared with most of the times?' Remind learners that median and mean must carry units: seconds, siblings.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured data comparison table (Observation Table): learners place mean, median and mode side by side for three data sets so patterns across cases become visible. Cumulative counting links to Lesson 2's ordered frequency lists and makes the median accessible from a frequency table without writing out all 40 values.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) learner orders the 7 times correctly before choosing the 4th value; (2) learner uses cumulative frequency to place the 20th and 21st values, writing 5, 14, 26, 34, 38, 40; (3) learner states the siblings median as 2 and the runner median as 106 s with units; (4) learner calculates 765/7 = 109.3 s correctly to 1 d.p. Use a quick exit slip question mid-lesson: 'Median of 3, 5, 9, 12?' (answer 7). Record who gets 7 and who gives 5 or 9.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4 learners discuss: (1) For the siblings data, why do mean, median and mode all give about 2? (2) For the runner times, why is the mean (109.3 s) larger than the median (106 s) and mode (105 s)? Which number would you give the selector? (3) What happened to the mean when the 130 s runner (who had a cold) was removed (109.3 s to 105.8 s)? What happened to the median (106 s to 105.5 s)? Which measure changed more? Groups draft a 'Choosing a Measure' rule such as: 'When the data has an extreme value (outlier), the median is more reliable than the mean; when the data is symmetrical with no outliers the three agree; for categories only the mode applies.' Learners then apply the rule to three quick cases and defend choices in writing: Mama Achieng's daily mandazi sales (40, 45, 42, 50, 65, 30, 20; total 292); the travel categories (Walk, Matatu, Boda boda, Bicycle, Private car, School bus); and the siblings table. They also link to the phenomenon: 'Why did Atieno say almost everyone walks when 14 of 40 is 35%? Which measure would the principal be given, and is it misleading?'
framework.teacherMoves: Pose: 'The 130 s runner had a cold. Should the coach delete that time to get a better number? Why or why not?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then groups of 4 discuss for 5 minutes. Use roles: reporter, recorder, checker, timekeeper. Cold-call 3 groups (use random cards) to present one claim, one piece of evidence and one reasoning link (Claim-Evidence-Reasoning). Press: 'Which number in the table supports your claim?' Challenge integrity: 'If we remove 130 s just because it is inconvenient, is that honest?' Guide learners to the idea that an outlier should be reported, not hidden, and that the median is a more resistant summary. For the mandazi data say: 'Order the 7 sales: 20, 30, 40, 42, 45, 50, 65. What is the median?' (42 mandazi; the mean is 292/7 = 41.7 mandazi). Ask: 'Here they are close. Why?' Link: 'For travel, can we find a median of Walk, Matatu, Boda boda? Why not?' Elicit that categories cannot be ordered numerically, so only the mode (Walk, 14 learners) applies. Ensure learners understand this about the class data only, not the whole school.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with argument from evidence: groups must state which measure best represents the runner data (claim), cite specific numbers (evidence: mean 109.3, median 106, mode 105, mean without outlier 105.8) and explain why one extreme value pulls the mean up (reasoning). Contrasting cases (siblings where measures agree versus runners where they differ) build a transferable rule rather than a memorised procedure.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for correct reasoning: 'the 130 s is much bigger than the others, so it pulls the mean up but the median stays in the middle'. Success criteria: the group names the outlier, quotes at least two numbers, and states a measure with a reason. Look for the misconception that the outlier should be deleted without justification; note groups that argue honestly for reporting it. Collect a 3-line exit response: 'For the runner data I would give the selector ___ because ___.' Check at least 75% choose the median (106 s) or explain the mean with the outlier.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board (started in Lesson 1) holding the question: 'How can we turn a messy list of data from our school into clear evidence that helps our principal make a fair decision?' On sticky notes they (1) add new questions that arose, for example 'Which measure would Mr Otieno need if we collected the siblings or fares data from the whole school?' and 'Can a graph show the outlier better than a number?'; (2) move or tick off earlier questions answered today, such as 'Why do the mean and the mode tell different stories?'; (3) write one 'What we now know' note, for example 'Median is the middle of ordered data; an outlier pulls the mean but not the median'. They group questions into categories: Summaries (done), Graphs (coming in Lessons 5 to 7), Fair decision (Lesson 8).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the DQB. Which of our questions did today's evidence help to answer? Walk to the board and place a green dot on it.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before learners move. Cold-call 3 learners to read out a question they added and say which lesson might answer it. Ask: 'Which measure will Mr Otieno use for how learners travel?' (the mode, Walk, because the data are categories). Point out that the principal also needs a clear picture, which leads to graphs. Keep a visible list titled 'Questions for Lesson 5: how do graphs show this?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a living record of learning: learners see which questions are answered by evidence and which remain open, linking each lesson to the overall problem. Categorising questions helps them recognise the whole statistics cycle (collect, organise, summarise, display, interpret).
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each learner has placed at least one new question or answer note. Look for questions that refer to evidence (numbers) rather than opinion. Note learners who connect median or outliers to Mr Otieno's decision, for example whether one unusual class could mislead him. Record the number of new questions about displaying data (graphs) to confirm readiness for Lesson 5.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class model, a flow diagram titled 'From messy list to fair decision', started in Lesson 1 and extended in Lessons 2 and 3. In their notebooks they add a new 'Summarise' box that now has three branches: Mode (most frequent; works for categories and numbers), Mean (Σfx ÷ Σf; uses every value; pulled by outliers) and Median (middle of ordered data; resists outliers). They add a decision arrow: 'Categories: use mode. Numbers with no extreme values: mean, median and mode are similar. Numbers with an outlier: report the median and mention the outlier.' They annotate the model with their own numbers: siblings (mean 2.1, median 2, mode 2) and runners (mean 109.3 s, median 106 s, mode 105 s, mean without 130 s 105.8 s). They finish with a 2-sentence note: 'What this means for Mr Otieno: ...'. They also write what the model still cannot do: show the pattern visually (to be solved with graphs).
framework.teacherMoves: Display the previous model. Say: 'Add today's learning. Where does the median fit? What decision arrow do we need?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before pair talk. Cold-call 3 learners to explain one branch of the model. Ask: 'Our class data cover only Grade 10 Green. What does that mean for how sure Mr Otieno can be?' Guide learners to the point that 40 learners is a small sample, so whole-school data are needed before deciding about the bus or lunch serving. Have learners complete the summary table prompts. Set a short follow-up task: 'Find the median of the 7 mandazi sales and say whether mean or median is better if Friday was a market day' (median 42; mean 41.7).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: learners extend an evolving diagram so that new ideas (median, outlier effect, choosing a measure) are linked to earlier ones (frequency table, mode, mean). Making the decision arrows explicit turns procedures into reasoning about which tool fits which data and question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that the revised model includes all three measures with a correct condition for choosing each. Success criteria: correct definitions, correct numbers (median 2 siblings; 106 s; mean 109.3 s; 105.8 s without 130 s), and one statement linking to Mr Otieno or the limits of one class. Use a short rubric: Exceeds (explains outlier effect with numbers and sample limits), Meets (correct measures and choice rule), Approaches (correct calculations but no reasoning), Below (errors in the median position).

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson ask yourself: Did learners order the data before finding the median, or did some pick the middle of an unordered list? How many used cumulative frequencies correctly for the 20th and 21st values? Did learners explain the outlier effect with numbers (109.3 versus 106 versus 105.8) or only say 'it is bigger'? Which learners still default to the mean as the 'best' measure? Did any learners tease peers about sibling numbers or running speed? What evidence shows learners understand that mean and median do not apply to travel categories? Plan to re-teach even-n medians (average of the two middle values) with 2 extra examples before Lesson 5 if more than a quarter of learners made errors.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We ordered the siblings data and found the 20th and 21st values both equal 2, so the median is 2 siblings (mean 2.1, mode 2). We ordered the 7 Eldoret club 800 m times and found the median 106 s, the mode 105 s and the mean 109.3 s; without the 130 s time the mean of the other six is 105.8 s.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The median is the middle value of ordered data (for odd n the ((n+1)/2)th value; for even n the mean of the two middle values). One very large or small value (an outlier) pulls the mean but hardly moves the median. For categories such as travel mode only the mode (Walk, 14 of 40) can be used.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The mean, median and mode agree for the siblings data because it is evenly spread, but they differ for the runner times because one slow time (130 s) pulls the mean up. So the best summary depends on the type of data and the question. For Mr Otieno this means choosing and explaining the measure honestly, and remembering that these data are from only one class.
