LESSONS.title: Bar graphs and line graphs: which picture fits which data?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: bar graph, line graph, categorical data, discrete data, change over time, frequency axis, scale, title, axis labels, trend, Mama Achieng, mandazi, Lakeview Senior School

slo.purpose: Learners draw a bar graph for the travel frequency table and a line graph for Mama Achieng's daily mandazi sales, then decide which graph suits which type of data, so that the principal's evidence is shown in a form that can be read at a glance.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (a) represent data using bar graphs and line graphs; (b) interpret data from bar graphs and line graphs; (c) appreciate the importance of data organisation and interpretation in making effective decisions. Key ideas: a bar graph (equal-width bars with gaps, frequency axis starting at 0, both axes labelled, with a title) suits categories such as Walk, Matatu, Boda boda, Bicycle, Private car, School bus. A line graph (points joined by straight lines, time on the horizontal axis) suits change over time such as daily mandazi sales.
slo.skills: Choosing a sensible scale (0 to 14 or 16 in steps of 2 for travel; 0 to 70 in steps of 10 for mandazi); plotting bars and points accurately on squared paper; labelling axes and giving a title; reading values and trends from a graph; justifying the choice of graph with evidence. NGSS-style practices embedded: Developing and Using Models (a graph is a model of the data), Analyzing and Interpreting Data, and Engaging in Argument from Evidence.
slo.attitudes: Core competency: Critical thinking and problem solving (interpretation and inference when representing data). Value: Integrity (honest, accurate plotting while working in groups). Value: Love (considerate of others when extracting information and drawing conclusions from graphs). PCI: Life Skills (Decision Making): making informed decisions by identifying patterns in graphs and drawing conclusions.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we use statistics in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 2 gave learners the travel frequency table (14, 12, 4, 3, 3, 4 = 40) and Lesson 4 showed that a summary should match the data. Lesson 5 turns the table into a bar graph so the class can see at a glance that Walk (14 of 40) is the largest group and Matatu (12 of 40) is second, so neither claim by Atieno or Brian shows a majority. It also introduces the line graph for data over time using the mandazi sales. The pie chart comes in Lesson 6 and critical reading of graphs in Lesson 7.
slo.safetyNotes: Learners use rulers and pencils, so remind them to carry sharp pencils and rulers safely and not to throw them. Arrange desks so that groups can share squared paper without crowding. If phones or tablets are used to check graphs, follow the school device rules. Data are only about travel mode and mandazi sales and use fictional names, so there are no privacy concerns.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Otieno still has money for only one of: a school bus route, a bicycle shed or a second lunch serving. The class has a frequency table, but a table of numbers is still hard to scan in a staff meeting. In this lesson Grade 10 Green at Lakeview Senior School, Kisumu, predicts which kind of picture would convince the principal fastest, draws a bar graph of the travel table (Walk 14, Matatu 12, Boda boda 4, Bicycle 3, Private car 3, School bus 4; total 40), then draws a line graph of Mama Achieng's mandazi sales at Kibuye market (Mon 40, Tue 45, Wed 42, Thu 50, Fri 65, Sat 30, Sun 20; total 292). They compare the two graphs and build a rule for which graph fits which data. They add questions to the DQB and revise their model of how raw data becomes evidence. The lesson builds on Lesson 2 (frequency tables) and Lesson 4 (a representation should match the data) and does not teach pie charts, which come in Lesson 6.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners are shown the travel frequency table from Lesson 2 (Walk 14, Matatu 12, Boda boda 4, Bicycle 3, Private car 3, School bus 4; total 40) on the board, with a second table of Mama Achieng's mandazi sales beside it (Mon 40, Tue 45, Wed 42, Thu 50, Fri 65, Sat 30, Sun 20). Individually, in their books, they sketch in 3 minutes the picture they think would help Mr Otieno most for the travel table, and a picture they think would suit the mandazi sales. They write one sentence: 'I think this graph fits because...'. Then they pair up and compare. Their predictions connect to the phenomenon: which picture will settle the claims 'Almost everyone walks' and 'Most of us come by matatu'?
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Mr Otieno will read your work in two minutes before a meeting. Sketch the picture you think shows him the travel evidence fastest. Then sketch one for Mama Achieng's mandazi sales. No rubbing out: this is a prediction.' Give 3 minutes of silent sketching. Say: 'Turn to your partner and explain WHY you chose that picture.' After 2 minutes, cold-call 4 pairs (not volunteers) to show their sketches without judging. Ask: 'Did anyone draw the same picture for both tables? Why or why not?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question before taking answers. Write the sketch types on the board (bars, line, others) without saying which is correct. Keep sketches visible for the Explain phase.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain with a Gallery of Initial Ideas: recording predictions before instruction makes learners' current thinking visible, so they notice later when the evidence confirms or changes it. Comparing sketches creates a real need to decide when to use bars and when to use a line.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) learners who sketch a picture for each table and give any reason; (2) whether they notice that travel mode is a list of categories while days follow each other in order; (3) misconceptions such as 'a line graph is always best because it looks neat' or 'bars without a starting zero are fine'. Record on a class list which learners chose the same type for both tables, and revisit these at the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A, bar graph (about 25 minutes). In groups of 4, learners use squared paper to draw a bar graph of the travel table. They choose a scale of 0 to 14 or 16 in steps of 2 on the frequency axis, start it at 0, draw 6 bars of equal width with equal gaps in the order Walk, Matatu, Boda boda, Bicycle, Private car, School bus, label both axes ('Means of travel', 'Number of learners') and write a title ('How Grade 10 Green travels to school, n = 40'). Each member plots 1 to 2 bars and checks a partner's bars against the table. They then read from their graph which bar is tallest (Walk, 14) and which two bars together reach 26 learners (Walk + Matatu = 65%). Part B, line graph (about 25 minutes). Learners draw a line graph of Mama Achieng's mandazi sales: days Mon to Sun on the horizontal axis, mandazi sold on the vertical axis from 0 to 70 in steps of 10, points plotted for each day and joined with straight lines, with axes labelled and a title. They note the highest day (Friday, 65), the lowest day (Sunday, 20), and the rise from Thursday 50 to Friday 65 followed by the fall to Saturday 30 and Sunday 20. Each group checks that the total of the plotted values is 292.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute squared paper, rulers and pencils (one set per group of 4). Model only the first bar on the board (Walk at height 14) and then step back. Circulate and say: 'Show me where your frequency axis starts. Why does it start at 0?' and 'Tell me how you decided the width of your bars.' Cold-call 3 groups to explain how they chose their scale. For the line graph say: 'Which axis shows time? Why does time go along the bottom?' Pose the question: 'If we join the travel bars with a line, from Walk to Matatu to Boda boda, would the line mean anything?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then take 3 responses. Do not give the answer yet. Check drawings against the established data: travel bars 14, 12, 4, 3, 3, 4 and mandazi points 40, 45, 42, 50, 65, 30, 20. Ask groups finished early: 'What does Mama Achieng learn from your line graph that she cannot see quickly in the table?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Constructing a model from evidence (Developing and Using Models): learners build each graph themselves from the table, so they see how every feature (starting at 0, equal bar widths, time on the horizontal axis) is a decision that affects how well the picture represents the data. Peer checking in groups builds accuracy and a shared language.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: frequency axis starts at 0 and uses equal steps; bars have equal width and gaps; all six bars match 14, 12, 4, 3, 3, 4; both axes and the title are present; line graph points match 40, 45, 42, 50, 65, 30, 20; learners can read Friday = 65 and Sunday = 20 and state that the bars total 40 and the sales total 292. Common errors to note: uneven scale, bars of different widths, leaving out axis labels, joining the travel bars with a line. Give a quick thumbs-up/sideways/down check on 'I can read my graph' before moving on.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners place their bar graph and line graph side by side and answer in groups: (1) What question does each graph answer? (2) Why would a line joining the travel bars be misleading? (3) Why do the mandazi points joined by a line make sense? (4) Which graph fits categorical data and which fits change over time? Groups write a class rule: 'Use a bar graph when... Use a line graph when...' with the travel and mandazi examples as evidence. Then they interpret the bar graph for Mr Otieno: Walk (14 of 40, 35%) is the tallest bar and Matatu (12 of 40, 30%) is second; neither is more than half, so 'almost everyone walks' and 'most of us come by matatu' are both wrong, though together they make 26 learners (65%). Bicycle is only 3 of 40 (7.5%) and School bus 4 of 40 (10%), so this class gives little support for a bicycle shed. Learners also note that the class bus count cannot confirm or refute Zawadi's remark that 'The bus is always full', because that is about the school's single 14-seater bus serving the whole school. They link back to Lesson 4: the picture must match the data, just as the best summary depends on the data.
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: 'Compare your two graphs. What is different about the data behind each one?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 learners from different groups. Ask: 'Mama Achieng wants to know if sales are rising or falling during the week. Which graph tells her? How do you know?' Then: 'Atieno said almost everyone walks. Use the tallest bar to test her claim: what fraction of the class walks?' Cold-call 3 learners and write 14/40 = 35% on the board. Ask: 'Is 35% almost everyone?' Press for evidence, not opinion: 'Point to the bar that shows it.' Ask: 'What does Zawadi's claim need that this class graph cannot give us?' Guide learners to the whole school and its single 14-seater bus. Keep the conclusion limited to Grade 10 Green. Compare their early predictions with what they have now drawn and ask: 'Whose prediction changed, and what changed it?' Do not teach pie charts: if a learner asks about circles, say 'Good question, we will park that on the DQB for Lesson 6.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with Think-Pair-Share: learners make a claim about which graph fits which data and support it with the specific bars and points they drew, then reason from the type of data (categories versus time). Using the graph to test Atieno's and Brian's claims shows that a good representation turns a messy list into evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: learners state that bar graphs suit categories (travel mode) and line graphs suit change over time (daily sales); they give a reason such as 'there is no order or in-between between Walk and Matatu, but Monday to Tuesday to Wednesday follows time'; they quote 14 of 40 = 35% and 12 of 40 = 30% from the bar heights; they say neither claim is more than half; they say the single class cannot settle the bus question. Use a quick exit slip: 'Name one data set for a bar graph and one for a line graph from your own life.' Mark acceptable examples (e.g. tree types at Lakeview, 30 trees: bar; a plant's height each week: line) and note learners who confuse the two.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board started in Lesson 1: 'How can we turn a messy list of data from our school into clear evidence that helps our principal make a fair decision?' Individually, they write one new question on a sticky note arising from today's graphs, for example 'Would the bars look the same for the whole school?', 'What if the bars started at 2 instead of 0?', 'Why can't we use a line for travel?' or 'How would a circle show the same travel data?'. They also move one earlier question to the 'partly answered' column with a note: for example 'Which picture shows the travel evidence best?' gets 'bar graph, from Lesson 5'. As a class they sort the new questions under headings such as 'Whole school data', 'Misleading graphs' and 'Other pictures'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Write one question that today's graphs made you wonder about. Put your name on the back.' Give 3 minutes of silent writing. Cold-call 5 learners to read their question aloud and place it on the DQB, asking each: 'Which part of the driving question does yours help with?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before each response. Point out the link to Lesson 7: 'Questions about axes that start at the wrong number will be answered when we read graphs critically.' Point out the link to Lesson 6: 'The circle question will be answered when we draw pie charts.' Invite learners to move answered questions to the 'we think we know' area with one line of evidence from today. Ask one learner to summarise: 'What do we know now that we did not know at the start of this lesson?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a living record of understanding: sorting questions into answered, partly answered and still open shows learners how their thinking has grown, gives them ownership of the investigation and sets a purpose for Lessons 6 and 7.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: questions refer to today's graphs and not just to earlier lessons; at least some questions go beyond the lesson, such as sample size, misleading axes or other picture types; learners can say which part of the driving question their question supports. Note learners who write only recall questions ('What is a bar graph?') and prompt them with 'What would you need to know to trust this graph?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class model that started in Lesson 1, a flow diagram of how raw data becomes evidence for Mr Otieno. They add the new step: 'Display: choose the graph that fits the data type' with two branches and examples, 'Categories (Walk, Matatu, Boda boda, Bicycle, Private car, School bus) = bar graph, bars separate, frequency axis from 0' and 'Change over time (Mon to Sun mandazi sales) = line graph, time along the bottom, points joined'. Beside each branch they sketch a mini bar graph and a mini line graph and write one sentence of evidence from today, for example 'The tallest bar is Walk at 14 of 40, 35%' and 'Mandazi sales peak on Friday at 65 and drop to 20 on Sunday'. They also add a caution box: 'One class is a small sample, so collect whole-school data before deciding on the bus or lunch serving'. Each learner writes a two-sentence note to Mr Otieno: what the bar graph says about a bicycle shed and what it cannot say about the bus.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the existing class model (raw list, tally, frequency table, mean/median/mode). Say: 'Add today's step. Where does a graph go in our model, and what decides which graph?' Give 5 minutes for groups to add it on poster paper. Cold-call 3 groups to present their added step and ask the others: 'Do you agree? What evidence from today supports it?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Ask: 'In our model, what still looks unfinished?' Guide learners to the pie chart and to checking graphs for tricks, then record both as 'To add' for Lessons 6 and 7. Collect the two-sentence notes to Mr Otieno as a written check. Finish with: 'Which would you trust more to show Mr Otieno the travel evidence, the raw list or the bar graph? Give me the evidence.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: learners add one new component to a shared model and justify it with data from this lesson, so each lesson builds a coherent explanation of how raw data become fair evidence and the model is open to further revision.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: the model has a display step with two branches that match graph type to data type; examples use the correct data (Walk 14, Matatu 12, Boda boda 4, Bicycle 3, Private car 3, School bus 4; mandazi 40, 45, 42, 50, 65, 30, 20); the note to Mr Otieno says the class gives little support for a bicycle shed (3 of 40, 7.5%) and that whole-school data are needed for the bus; learners do not claim the bus is full or empty from the class data. Note learners who still apply a line to categories and reteach with a quick question: 'Is there a value between Walk and Matatu?'

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) Did learners start the frequency axis at 0 and keep bars equal in width, or did some need reminding? (2) Could learners explain why a line does not make sense for travel categories, or did they only repeat the rule? (3) Which predictions from the Predict phase changed and why? (4) Did any learner use the bar graph to say that the class proves what the whole school does, or that Zawadi's claim about the bus is settled? Plan a quick correction if so. (5) Which learners need more practice with scales on squared paper before Lesson 6, where angles and a protractor are used, and before Lesson 7, where axes are examined critically? Keep a note of questions on the DQB that you can answer in those lessons.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Bar graph of travel: Walk 14, Matatu 12, Boda boda 4, Bicycle 3, Private car 3, School bus 4 (total 40), with the tallest bar for Walk. Line graph of Mama Achieng's mandazi sales: Mon 40, Tue 45, Wed 42, Thu 50, Fri 65, Sat 30, Sun 20, peaking on Friday and falling to Sunday.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: A bar graph suits categories, with separate equal-width bars and a frequency axis starting at 0. A line graph suits change over time, with time on the horizontal axis and points joined by straight lines. Both need labelled axes and a title.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The same table of travel data becomes clear evidence in a bar graph: Walk is 14 of 40 (35%) and Matatu is 12 of 40 (30%), so neither claim shows a majority, though together they are 65%. Bicycle (3 of 40) gives little support for a shed. We should choose the graph that matches the data type, and collect whole-school data before deciding on the bus or lunch serving.

LESSONS.title: Pie charts: turning frequencies into angles
LESSONS.aresKeywords: pie chart, sector, angle, frequency, total frequency, 360 degrees, protractor, percentage, proportion, bar graph comparison, family budget

slo.purpose: Learners convert frequencies into angles using f / n x 360, draw and label pie charts for the Grade 10 Green travel data and the Wanjiru family budget, and compare a pie chart with the bar graph of the same data to decide which representation best answers Mr Otieno's question.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (c) represent data using pie charts; (d) interpret data from pie charts. Learners will know that a pie chart shows each category as a share of a whole (the total frequency n), that the angles must add up to 360 degrees, and that a pie chart is best for 'how much of the whole?' while a bar graph is best for comparing exact counts.
slo.skills: Calculating angle = f / n x 360 degrees (for travel data 360 / 40 = 9 degrees per learner); using a protractor to draw sectors accurately; labelling sectors with category, frequency and percentage; checking that angles sum to 360; comparing representations of the same data; communicating a data-based claim. NGSS-style practices: analysing and interpreting data, using mathematics and computational thinking, constructing explanations, and engaging in argument from evidence.
slo.attitudes: Appreciate the importance of data organisation and interpretation in making effective decisions (KICD SLO e). Values: Integrity - learners are honest when measuring and recording angles; Love - learners are considerate of others when working with peers to extract information from charts and draw conclusions. Core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving (interpretation and inference); Digital literacy (optional use of a phone or tablet spreadsheet to check the chart). PCI: Life Skills (Decision Making) - informed decisions from patterns in charts.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we use statistics in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 2 gave us the frequency table and percentages (Walk 14, Matatu 12, Boda boda 4, Bicycle 3, Private car 3, School bus 4 = 40). Lesson 5 gave us the bar graph of the same data. Now learners draw the pie chart, so they can see walk (126 degrees) and matatu (108 degrees) as shares of the whole class, and decide which graph helps the principal most. This moves the driving question forward: the same data in a different form can show a different thing clearly. Lesson 7 will then ask how to read graphs critically.
slo.safetyNotes: Compasses and protractors have sharp points: carry them point-down, never point at others, and return them to the box. Keep the desk clear when drawing circles. If using phones or tablets offline, share devices fairly and keep bags off the floor walkways. Remind learners that the class data covers only Grade 10 Green and the names are fictional, so no learner should be teased about how they travel.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Otieno still has money for only one of: a school bus route, a bicycle shed or a second lunch serving. In earlier lessons Grade 10 Green organised their 40 travel responses into a frequency table and drew a bar graph. In this lesson learners predict how the 360 degrees of a circle should be shared among the six travel groups, discover that each learner is worth 360 / 40 = 9 degrees, and calculate and draw the travel pie chart (Walk 126, Matatu 108, Boda boda 36, Bicycle 27, Private car 27, School bus 36 = 360). They then apply the same method to the Wanjiru family monthly budget of KSh 30,000 in Nairobi (Food 144, Rent 90, School fees 54, Transport 36, Savings 36 = 360). Finally they compare the pie chart and bar graph of the travel data and decide when each is the better evidence. They see that walking and matatu together take 65% of the circle (234 degrees), neither is more than half, and the bicycle sector is small, which still gives little support for a shed from this one class.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sit in groups of four. Mr Kamau shows a blank circle on the board and says it stands for all 40 learners in Grade 10 Green. Without any calculation, each learner sketches on a sheet how they think the circle should be cut for Walk, Matatu, Boda boda, Bicycle, Private car and School bus, using the earlier claims (Atieno: 'Almost everyone walks'; Brian: 'Most of us come by matatu') as a guide. They write one sentence: 'I predict the biggest slice is ___ because ___.' They also predict: 'If the whole circle is 360 degrees, how many degrees might ONE learner be worth?' Groups share their sketches by holding them up. This connects to the phenomenon: the same 40 responses that looked meaningless as a raw list can now be seen as slices of a whole.
framework.teacherMoves: Draw a large circle and say: 'This whole circle is our whole class of 40. Before I give you any numbers, sketch how you think it should be shared. Do not calculate, just predict.' Give 3 minutes of silent individual work. WAIT TIME: after asking 'What do you think one learner is worth in degrees?', wait 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 4 learners (2 who predicted walk, 1 who predicted matatu, 1 who predicted something else) with: 'Tell us your biggest slice and your reason.' Do not say who is correct. Record 3 or 4 predictions on the board under 'Our predictions'. Ask: 'Could one slice be more than half the circle? What would that mean in learners?' Collect the sketches to compare later.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with reasoning (individual first, then share): writing a prediction and a reason before instruction exposes prior ideas, such as 'the biggest slice must be more than half', and gives learners a personal stake in checking their prediction against the calculated chart later.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether learners (1) draw slices of different sizes rather than equal ones, (2) link slice size to the number of learners, and (3) give a reason, not just a guess. Note learners who think the circle has 40 degrees or 100 degrees. Tick on a class list who predicted walk, matatu or other. Listen for the idea of a 'whole' and its 'parts'.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups receive the frequency table from Lesson 2 (Walk 14, Matatu 12, Boda boda 4, Bicycle 3, Private car 3, School bus 4; total 40), a protractor, a ruler, a compass, plain paper and a calculation worksheet. Step 1: they find the angle for one learner, 360 / 40 = 9 degrees. Step 2: they complete the table using angle = f / n x 360: Walk 14 x 9 = 126, Matatu 12 x 9 = 108, Boda boda 36, Bicycle 27, Private car 27, School bus 36. Step 3: they add the angles and check the sum is 360 degrees. They also add a percentage column (35%, 30%, 10%, 7.5%, 7.5%, 10%) and see that percentage x 3.6 gives the same angle. Step 4: they draw a circle of radius 5 cm, mark a starting radius, and use a protractor to draw each sector in the order Walk, Matatu, Boda boda, Bicycle, Private car, School bus. Step 5: they label each sector with the category, frequency and percentage, and give the chart a title. Groups swap charts and check each other's angles with a protractor. Early finishers repeat for the Wanjiru budget angles (144, 90, 54, 36, 36).
framework.teacherMoves: Demonstrate one sector on the board: 'Watch my hands. I place the protractor centre on the circle centre, line up the zero line with my starting radius, and mark 126 degrees. Where do I begin the next sector?' Circulate and ask each group: 'How did you get 27 degrees for Bicycle? Show me the working.' Cold-call 3 groups to give the angle for a different category without looking at the answer line. WAIT TIME: after asking 'Why must all the angles add to 360?', wait 10-15 seconds before taking responses. Common errors to watch for: reading the wrong scale on the protractor (inner versus outer), starting each new sector from the circle edge rather than the last radius, and angles that sum to 359 or 361 because of rounding. Say: 'If your total is not 360, find the mistake before you draw.' Remind: 'Sharp points down, please.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Stepwise worked procedure with peer checking: learners connect the proportion idea (14 out of 40) to the angle (14 out of 40 of 360) through a calculation table, then check one another's constructions. Using the total-equals-360 check builds the idea that the pie chart is a whole divided into parts, linking back to the percentages from Lesson 2.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check (1) angles calculated correctly using f / n x 360, (2) the sum of angles equals 360, (3) sectors drawn within 2 degrees of the true value, (4) sectors in the correct order, (5) title and labels present. Use a quick checklist: Calculation / Accuracy / Labels. Note groups who use 9 degrees per learner as a shortcut and ask them to explain why it works only for n = 40.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners lay their travel pie chart next to the bar graph of the same data from Lesson 5. In groups they complete a comparison table with three columns: 'Easier to see on the pie chart', 'Easier to see on the bar graph' and 'Same on both'. They answer: (1) Is the Walk slice more than half the circle? (126 is less than 180). (2) Which two sectors together are almost two-thirds of the circle? (Walk + Matatu = 234 degrees = 65%). (3) What can the bar graph show that the pie chart cannot show easily? (exact counts, and comparing Bicycle 3 with Private car 3). They then repeat the reasoning for the Wanjiru family budget pie chart: Food takes 144 degrees (40%), more than Rent (90 degrees, 25%). In a class talk they write a two-sentence claim for Mr Otieno: 'On this evidence from Grade 10 Green, ___. But because ___, we should ___.' They revisit Atieno's and Brian's claims and decide, using angles, that neither is more than half. They note that Zawadi's remark about the bus cannot be tested with this class data.
framework.teacherMoves: Pose: 'Atieno said almost everyone walks. Use your pie chart to give evidence for or against.' Give 1 minute silent think time, then 10-15 seconds WAIT TIME after asking 'What fraction of the circle would almost everyone be?' Cold-call 4 learners with different views and use the stems: 'I notice ___', 'The angle shows ___', 'I disagree because ___'. Ask: 'If the principal only had 10 seconds, which graph would you hand him? Why?' Press for reasoning with 'How do you know?' and 'What would change your mind?'. Probe sampling: 'Does this class speak for the whole school?' Guide towards the recommendation: no money for a shed on this evidence, and collect whole-school data before deciding on the bus or lunch serving. Do not teach misleading axes yet; that is for Lesson 7.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Compare-and-contrast of representations plus claim-evidence-reasoning: learners place two displays of the same data side by side to see that each shows something different, then write a claim supported by angle and percentage evidence. This builds the understanding that the best representation depends on the question being asked.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for learners who (1) use angles or percentages as evidence rather than just 'it looks big', (2) correctly say that no sector is over 180 degrees so no travel mode is more than half, (3) state one advantage of each graph, and (4) mention that one class is a small sample. Collect the two-sentence claims as an exit slip and sort them into 'evidence-based', 'partly' and 'opinion only'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board headed 'How can we turn a messy list of data from our school into clear evidence that helps our principal make a fair decision?' On sticky notes they add new questions that came from the pie chart, such as 'Would the pie chart look the same for the whole school?', 'Can a pie chart be used for the runner times or the siblings data?', 'What if two sectors are almost equal?', and 'How could someone make a pie chart look unfair?'. They place their notes under headings such as 'Collecting', 'Organising', 'Summarising', 'Displaying' and 'Deciding'. They also move one earlier question, such as 'How can we see who is right?', to an 'Answered' area and attach their pie chart as evidence.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at your pie chart. What does it let us answer now? What new question does it make you ask?' Give 2 minutes silent writing, then 10-15 seconds WAIT TIME before anyone shares. Cold-call 3 learners to read a note aloud and say where it goes on the board. Ask: 'Which of these questions can we answer next lesson?' Link: 'The question about unfair graphs, we will come back to in Lesson 7.' Photograph or record the DQB for the next lesson.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board questioning: learners turn what they have just learned into new questions and sort them, which keeps the inquiry connected to the principal's decision and shows how each lesson adds to the evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that questions are linked to the pie chart or the decision (not unrelated), that learners can say which step of the statistics cycle the question belongs to, and that at least some questions go beyond simple recall (for example about fairness or sample size). Note which learners are ready to move an earlier question to 'Answered'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open their class model, started in Lesson 1 and revised since, on how to turn a messy list into evidence. In groups they add a new section called 'Display as a share of the whole: pie chart' with: (1) the formula angle = f / n x 360, (2) the check that angles sum to 360, (3) a small labelled travel pie chart (Walk 126, Matatu 108, Boda boda 36, Bicycle 27, Private car 27, School bus 36), and (4) a note on when a pie chart is a good choice (parts of a whole, few categories) and when a bar graph is better (exact counts, comparing close values). They also add a short rule of thumb: 'Pie chart for shares of a total such as the Wanjiru family KSh 30,000 budget; bar graph for comparing counts.' Then they complete the summary table in their books, revising their earlier claim to Mr Otieno.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your model. What new piece does the pie chart add to how we turn messy data into evidence?' Ask each group to explain one new arrow or box. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after 'Where in our model does the total 40 matter?' Cold-call 3 groups to share their rule of thumb and challenge it: 'Would a pie chart work for 15 different tree types? Why or why not?' Prompt revision: 'Has anything in your first model changed because of what you drew today?' Remind them the whole school must be surveyed before a final decision on the bus or lunch serving. Collect the models and the summary tables.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: learners add the pie chart step to their evolving model of the statistics cycle and explain how it connects to frequency tables, bar graphs and the principal's decision. This consolidates the idea that each step transforms the data into clearer evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for models that (1) include the formula f / n x 360 and the 360 check, (2) link the pie chart to the frequency table and total n, (3) state when a pie chart or bar graph is better, and (4) connect to the decision for Mr Otieno. Use a 3-level check: Not yet (formula only), Developing (formula plus drawing), Secure (formula, drawing and reasoned choice of representation).

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Did learners explain WHY angle = f / n x 360 works, or did they only follow the steps? How many struggled with the protractor and how could that be supported next time (for example, a cut-out 9-degree wedge)? Did the pie chart versus bar graph comparison lead to reasoned choices rather than a simple preference? Did anyone notice that a slice below 180 degrees means less than half? Which learners used percentages and angles as evidence in their claims? Were any learners uncomfortable about how they travel to school, and how can the discussion remain respectful? Note questions on the DQB that need to be picked up in Lesson 7, especially fairness of graphs, and plan how to use them.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that the 40 travel responses can be shown as a pie chart: Walk 126 degrees, Matatu 108 degrees, Boda boda 36 degrees, Bicycle 27 degrees, Private car 27 degrees and School bus 36 degrees, which add up to 360 degrees. Walk takes 14 of 40 learners (35%) and Matatu 12 of 40 (30%), so together 65%, but neither is more than half the circle. We also drew the Wanjiru family budget of KSh 30,000 (Food 144, Rent 90, School fees 54, Transport 36, Savings 36 = 360).
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that angle = f / n x 360, that each learner in our class is worth 9 degrees, that the angles of a pie chart must add up to 360, and that a pie chart shows each part as a share of the whole while a bar graph shows exact counts and is better for comparing close values.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain that the pie chart helps Mr Otieno see at a glance that walking and matatu are the biggest groups but neither is the majority, and that only 3 of 40 (7.5%) cycle, so this class gives little support for a bicycle shed. Because this is only one class, we advise collecting the same data from the whole school before deciding on the bus or second lunch serving.

LESSONS.title: Reading Graphs Critically and Using Digital Tools
LESSONS.aresKeywords: interpret graph, conclusion, evidence, misleading graph, truncated axis, scale, spreadsheet, digital tool, bar graph, pie chart, line graph

slo.purpose: Learners read bar graphs, line graphs and pie charts to extract information and defend conclusions with numbers, spot a misleading graph whose vertical axis starts at 2 instead of 0, and recreate a graph using a spreadsheet or graphing app, so they can give Mr Otieno trustworthy evidence.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (d) interpret data from bar graphs, line graphs and pie charts; (c) represent data using bar graphs, line graphs and pie charts on a digital device; (e) appreciate the importance of data organisation and interpretation in making effective decisions. Learners know that a bar graph's frequency axis must start at 0, and that a truncated axis makes walk (14) look 12 times bicycle (3) when the true ratio is 14:3, about 4.7 times.
slo.skills: Extracting information from graphs and charts, drawing and defending conclusions with numbers, comparing a graph with its frequency table to detect distortion, and entering data and creating labelled graphs on a spreadsheet or app (SEP: Analysing and interpreting data; Engaging in argument from evidence; Using mathematics and computational thinking).
slo.attitudes: Core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving (interpretation and inference when reading graphs); Digital literacy (using a digital device to draw graphs and charts). Values: Integrity (honest graphs, truthful scales); Love (considerate when working with peers to extract information and draw conclusions). PCI: Life Skills (Decision Making), making informed decisions by identifying patterns in graphs and drawing conclusions.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we use statistics in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 5 and 6 taught learners to draw the bar graph, line graph and pie chart. Lesson 4 taught them that the best measure depends on the data. In Lesson 7 they stop drawing and start judging: can a graph be trusted, and what exactly does it let us claim? This prepares the final recommendation to Mr Otieno in Lesson 8. Walk 14 (35%) and Matatu 12 (30%) together make 65%. Bicycle is 3 (7.5%) and School bus 4 (10%). Only one class is covered, so conclusions must be limited.
slo.safetyNotes: Handle phones, tablets and computers carefully, share devices fairly and keep chargers away from water. Work offline with the installed spreadsheet or graphing app; do not browse the internet. Keep bags and cables out of walkways. Learners who use a phone should not share personal information or photographs. Rulers and protractors are used with care.

LESSONS.overview: Mr Kamau shows Grade 10 Green of Lakeview Senior School, Kisumu, two bar graphs of the same travel data, one with the axis starting at 0 and one starting at 2. Learners predict which one tells the truth about walking and cycling, then, working in pairs, examine four graphs: the honest travel bar graph, the misleading one (walk 12 units, bicycle 1 unit, apparently 12 times, truly 14:3), the travel pie chart (angles 126, 108, 36, 27, 27, 36 = 360) and Mama Achieng's mandazi line graph (Mon 40, Tue 45, Wed 42, Thu 50, Fri 65, Sat 30, Sun 20, total 292). Pairs extract facts, write one conclusion each with a number to back it up, and say what a graph cannot show, such as Zawadi's claim about the school's single 14-seater bus, which a count of 4 learners from one class cannot confirm or refute. They then recreate the travel bar graph and pie chart on a spreadsheet or app and test what happens when the axis start is changed. The lesson ends by adding to the Driving Question Board and revising the class model of how messy data becomes fair evidence for Mr Otieno.

framework.learnerExperience: Mr Kamau projects or draws two bar graphs of the same Grade 10 Green travel data side by side without the frequency table. Graph A has the vertical axis starting at 0. Graph B has it starting at 2. Individually, learners write for 2 minutes: 'Which graph tells the truth about how many more learners walk than cycle? How many times taller is the Walk bar than the Bicycle bar in each graph?' They sketch a prediction and then compare with a partner. They are not yet told the answer. Link: the principal may see only one graph, so which one he sees may change his decision.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Mr Otieno has a busy day and will look at only one of these graphs for ten seconds. Study both quietly and decide which one he should trust.' Give 2 minutes of silent writing. Then say: 'Turn to your partner and compare for one minute.' Cold-call 4 pairs for their prediction and reason, without confirming or correcting. Ask: 'What would you check to be sure?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after each question before calling on anyone. Record the predictions in a tally on the board (A is true, B is true, both are true, cannot tell). Say: 'Keep your prediction, we will test it with the evidence.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-before-instruction with a Notice and Wonder frame. Committing to a written prediction exposes the common idea that a taller bar always means a bigger number, creating a need to check the scale. Recording the vote publicly gives the class a claim to revisit, which builds the habit of testing a graph instead of trusting the picture.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) learners who write a tallest-bar ratio rather than only 'it looks bigger'; (2) learners who mention the starting number on the axis, or ask for the table; (3) learners with the misconception that both graphs are equally true because 'the bars are there'. Tally the votes and note the 3 pairs who raise the axis, as evidence for who to call on later.

framework.learnerExperience: Pairs receive a Graph Detective sheet with four displays from Grade 10 Green and Mama Achieng's data: (1) the honest travel bar graph (axis 0 to 16, steps of 2); (2) the misleading bar graph (axis starting at 2); (3) the travel pie chart; (4) the mandazi line graph for Mon to Sun. For each, the pair completes: 'What does the title and each axis tell us? Read three exact values. Write one conclusion with a number.' On Graph 1 they read Walk 14, Matatu 12, Boda boda 4, Bicycle 3, Private car 3, School bus 4. On Graph 2 they measure bar heights: Walk 12 units, Bicycle 1 unit, so apparently 12 times, and compare with the true 14 to 3, about 4.7 times (14 ÷ 3 = 4.67). On Graph 3 they use the angles to check: 126 ÷ 360 = 35% for Walk and 126 + 108 = 234 degrees, which is 65% for Walk plus Matatu. On Graph 4 they find Friday highest (65), Sunday lowest (20), total 292, and the rise from Thursday 50 to Friday 65 and the fall to Saturday 30. They also write one question each graph cannot answer, for example 'Is the school bus always full?', since only 4 of the 40 in this class use it and the school has a single 14-seater bus serving the whole school.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the sheets and say: 'You are graph detectives. Every claim needs a number from the graph.' Circulate and ask each pair: 'Show me where on the graph you got that value.' At Graph 2, ask: 'Measure the Walk and Bicycle bars. How many times taller is Walk? Now divide the real frequencies, 14 by 3. Do the answers agree?' Point learners who stall to the axis start. For the pie chart, ask: 'How can you use degrees to check the percentage? What fraction of 360 is 126?' For the line graph, ask: 'Which two days show the largest change? What might explain it at Kibuye market?' For Zawadi's bus claim, ask: 'Can this graph prove the bus is always full? What other data would we need?' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before offering hints. Give 20 minutes. Stop and cold-call 5 pairs, each reading one value and one conclusion.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence-based reading with Claim-Evidence-Limit sentence frames: 'I claim ... because the graph shows ... but the graph cannot tell us ...'. Cross-checking one graph against another (pie against bar, bar against table) lets learners find the distortion themselves and builds argument from evidence about what a graph can and cannot support.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) learners read exact values rather than estimates, for example Walk 14 and Bicycle 3; (2) they compute 14 ÷ 3 ≈ 4.7 and compare with 12; (3) they convert 126 degrees to 35% correctly; (4) each conclusion includes a number; (5) they name a limit such as 'one class only' or 'cannot say about the bus'. Check sheets for pairs who give conclusions without numbers, and note which pairs misread the axis scale.

framework.learnerExperience: Whole-class discussion. Pairs share what they found and agree on a rule: how to spot a misleading graph. They list checks such as: does the frequency axis start at 0? Are the steps equal? Are both axes and the title labelled? Are bars the same width? Do the pie angles add to 360? Then they defend conclusions for Mr Otieno using the honest graphs: walking is the largest group (14 of 40, 35%) and matatu second (12 of 40, 30%); 'almost everyone walks' and 'most come by matatu' are both wrong because neither is more than half, though together they are 26 learners, 65%. Only 3 of 40 (7.5%) cycle, so this class gives little support for a bicycle shed. Learners connect to Lesson 4: for travel categories only the mode (Walk, 14) applies, since mean and median do not apply to categories. They also discuss which display suits which question: the pie chart for parts of the whole, the bar graph for comparing categories, the line graph for change over time. Digital part: pairs open a spreadsheet or graphing app on a shared device, type the travel frequency table (Walk 14, Matatu 12, Boda boda 4, Bicycle 3, Private car 3, School bus 4), create a bar graph and a pie chart, add a title and axis labels, then change the axis minimum from 0 to 2 and observe how the bars change. They check that the pie chart percentages match 35%, 30%, 10%, 7.5%, 7.5%, 10%.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Tell me one check that stops us being fooled by a graph.' Cold-call 6 learners, one check each, and list them on the board. WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds. Ask: 'Why might someone draw the axis from 2? Was it dishonest or just careless? What should an honest data person do?' Link to Integrity. Ask: 'Atieno said almost everyone walks. Use the graph to say whether she is right, with a number.' Cold-call 3 pairs. Ask: 'Can we tell Mr Otieno to build a bicycle shed?' and 'Can one class decide the bus or lunch serving?' Guide to the conclusion that the data covers only Grade 10 Green and the whole school must be surveyed. For the digital task, model the first step only: entering the table, then circulate. Say: 'Change the axis minimum to 2 and watch Walk and Bicycle. What changed, and what did not change in the data?' Share devices so every learner types or reads at least once. Remind them: no internet needed.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Argument from evidence, with a Consensus Discussion and a class-built checklist. The checklist turns noticing into a reusable criterion for critical reading. Changing the axis on the digital tool is a manipulation experiment: the data stays fixed, only the display changes, so learners see that the picture, not the numbers, is what is misleading. This builds their understanding of which summary and graph to trust.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: (1) learners state at least three checks, including axis starting at 0; (2) they use numbers (14, 12, 35%, 65%, 7.5%) in defending conclusions; (3) they say the data covers one class only; (4) on the device, the graph has a title, labelled axes and correct values; (5) they explain that changing the axis changes the look but not the data. Use a 3-question exit ticket: 'Why should a bar graph start at 0? Walk 14, Bicycle 3: what is the true ratio? What would you tell Mr Otieno about a bicycle shed?' Look for 14:3 or about 4.7 times.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board: 'How can we turn a messy list of data from our school into clear evidence that helps our principal make a fair decision?' In pairs they write on sticky notes: (1) one answered question, for example 'Why did the second graph make walking look so much bigger? Because the axis started at 2'; (2) one new question, for example 'How many learners must we ask in the whole school before we trust the results?' or 'How should we report that the bus claim cannot be checked from our class?'. They place the notes on the board under headings such as Reading Graphs, Honest Graphs, Digital Tools and Still Unsure.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Write one thing you can now answer and one thing you still want to know.' Give 3 minutes. Cold-call 4 pairs to read a note aloud and place it. WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds. Ask: 'Which question will be most important for the final recommendation to Mr Otieno?' Point out that Lesson 8 will pull all the evidence together. Move answered notes to an Answered area and keep open questions visible. Praise notes that carry a number or a limit.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question tracking using the DQB. Sorting notes into answered and open questions makes learning visible and helps learners see how Lesson 7 moves them from making graphs to judging evidence, and which gaps remain before they can advise the principal.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: (1) at least 70% of pairs post one answered and one new question; (2) new questions mention the sample size, the type of graph, or fairness; (3) answered notes use correct terms such as axis, scale, frequency. Note any pairs whose questions still show confusion about the axis, for revisiting at the start of Lesson 8.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open the class model of how messy data becomes fair evidence: raw list of 40 responses, then tally and frequency table (Lesson 2), then summaries (modes, means, medians in Lessons 3 and 4), then displays (bar, line and pie in Lessons 5 and 6). They add a new final stage: 'Check the display is honest and read it carefully'. In pairs they add a Graph Checklist box (axis starts at 0, equal steps, title, labels, angles sum to 360, claim has a number, state the limit) and a 'Limits' arrow showing that one class cannot speak for the whole school. They revise their draft model and write a 2-sentence note: 'The principal can trust a graph if ... . For our data, he should not ... because ... .' They add to the summary table what was observed, learned and explained.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model has a new stage today. Where does it go and why?' Give pairs 5 minutes to revise the model, then cold-call 3 pairs to explain a change. WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds. Ask: 'If Mr Otieno saw the misleading graph first, which decision might he make and what would that cost the school?' Ask: 'Which display would you give him for the travel data and why?' Expect: bar graph or pie chart, with the table beside it. Check that models keep the numbers exact: 14, 12, 4, 3, 3, 4 = 40; 35%, 30%, 65%. Encourage learners to note a gap for Lesson 8: the whole-school data needed before choosing the bus or lunch serving.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision. Adding a critical-reading stage to the model helps learners integrate organising, summarising, displaying and judging into one process, and prepares them to build their final recommendation in Lesson 8. Writing a short explanatory note forces them to connect the model to the evidence and the principal's decision.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: (1) the revised model includes a checking-the-graph stage and a limits arrow; (2) the 2-sentence note states that the axis must start at 0 and that the bicycle shed is not supported by this class data (3 of 40, 7.5%); (3) numbers in the model match the anchor data; (4) learners say the whole school should be surveyed. Collect models and use the checklist to decide who needs extra support before the Lesson 8 project.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: Did learners find the axis problem themselves by comparing the 12 units to 1 unit with the true 14 to 3, or did they need me to point it out? Which pairs wrote conclusions with numbers and limits, and which only described the picture? Were devices shared fairly, and did every learner enter or read data at the spreadsheet? Which learners still believe a taller bar always means a bigger number? What will I revisit at the start of Lesson 8 so every pair can make a fair, data-based recommendation to Mr Otieno?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that the same travel data looked very different on two bar graphs: with the axis starting at 0, Walk (14) is about 4.7 times Bicycle (3); with the axis starting at 2, Walk looked 12 times Bicycle. We also read the pie chart and the mandazi line graph, and recreated the travel graphs on a spreadsheet or app.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned to read exact values from bar graphs, pie charts and line graphs, to support every conclusion with a number, and to check a graph for a frequency axis that starts at 0, equal steps, labels, a title and pie angles that add to 360. We also learned that one class cannot speak for the whole school.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: A misleading graph changes how the data looks, not the data itself. Honest graphs of the travel data show Walk 14 of 40 (35%) and Matatu 12 of 40 (30%), together 65%, and only 3 of 40 (7.5%) cycling, so the class gives little support for a bicycle shed. Mr Otieno should trust a graph only after checking its axis and scale, and should collect whole-school data before deciding on the bus or lunch serving.
