LESSONS.title: Project: Evidence for the Principal
LESSONS.aresKeywords: statistics cycle, evidence, recommendation, frequency table, mean median mode, bar graph, pie chart, sample, misleading graph, final explanation, Driving Question Board

slo.purpose: To synthesise the whole statistics cycle (collect, organise, summarise, display, interpret) into a data-based recommendation for Mr Otieno and to answer the driving question. No new technique is taught.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the sub strand, the learner should be able to: a) draw a frequency distribution table for ungrouped data; b) determine mean, mode and median of ungrouped data; c) represent data using bar graphs, line graphs and pie charts; d) interpret data from bar graphs, line graphs and pie charts; e) appreciate the importance of data organization and interpretation in making effective decisions.
slo.skills: Communication and collaboration; Critical thinking and problem solving: interpretation and inference when drawing conclusions from the Grade 10 Green travel data. Digital literacy: using a spreadsheet or graphing app (offline-capable) to display data. Science and Engineering Practices: analysing and interpreting data; constructing explanations; engaging in argument from evidence; developing and using models.
slo.attitudes: Integrity: honest reporting of what the data does and does not show. Love: consideration of others when peers present and critique. Life Skills (Decision Making): making informed decisions from patterns in graphs and charts.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we use statistics in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1 to 7 moved from an unsettled raw list (Lesson 1), to frequency tables (2), mean, mode and median (3-4), bar, line and pie graphs (5-6), and critical reading of graphs and digital tools (7). In Lesson 8 learners bring every step together, present recommendations to Mr Otieno, compare the Lesson 1 draft model with the final model, and complete the DQB to answer: How can we turn a messy list of data from our school into clear evidence that helps our principal make a fair decision?
slo.safetyNotes: Learners use only their own anonymous class travel data; no names are linked to responses. Treat all peer presentations with respect and critique the evidence, not the person. Phones or tablets: use offline, keep volume low, and follow school device rules. Protractors and compasses: carry with points down.

LESSONS.overview: Lakeview Senior School in Kisumu: Mr Otieno has money for only one of a school bus route, a bicycle shed or a second lunch serving. In Lesson 1 Atieno said 'Almost everyone walks', Brian said 'Most of us come by matatu', and Zawadi said 'The bus is always full', and the raw list of 40 responses settled nothing. Today Grade 10 Green finishes the project. Groups run the full cycle on the anchor data (Walk 14, Matatu 12, Boda boda 4, Bicycle 3, Private car 3, School bus 4; total 40) and present an evidence-based recommendation: walking is the largest group (35%), matatu second (30%), together 65%; neither is more than half, so both claims are wrong; bicycle is only 7.5% and school bus 10%, so no money for a shed on this evidence; and because one class is a small sample, collect the same data from the whole school before deciding on the bus or lunch serving. Zawadi's claim concerns the single 14-seater bus serving the whole school, so 4 learners on the bus in this class can neither confirm nor refute it. Learners also use siblings and runner times to explain why the best summary depends on the data type. They then compare the Lesson 1 draft model with a final model, complete the DQB and write the Final Explanation.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall Lesson 1 when the list of 40 responses could not settle the claims of Atieno, Brian and Zawadi. On a sticky note or in their books they write a prediction: 'If I give Mr Otieno ONE page of evidence, what should be on it, and what should his decision be about the bicycle shed?' They also predict which claim, 'Almost everyone walks' or 'Most of us come by matatu', will survive the full analysis. They privately rate their confidence from 1 to 5. They share with a partner for 2 minutes, then with the class.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the Lesson 1 draft model and the DQB on the board. Say: 'Three weeks ago we could not tell who was right. Today you are the statisticians advising Mr Otieno. Before we open any tables, write your prediction.' Give WAIT TIME of 15 seconds of silence. Cold-call 4 learners for predictions: 'Wanjiru, what would you put on the one page? Why?' Record predictions without judging. Ask: 'What would make Mr Otieno trust your page?' Do NOT reveal the totals yet; keep Walk 14, Matatu 12 and the rest hidden until learners retrieve them from their own work in the Observe Phase.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with confidence rating and Think-Pair-Share: surfaces prior ideas about how data becomes evidence, so learners can compare their starting ideas with their final model and see their own growth.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: predictions that mention organising data (table), a display (graph or chart) and a summary, not just 'count them'; learners who name 'whole school' or 'more data'; learners who still predict one claim is simply right. Tally how many name each statistics step; reteach any step missing in the groups' later work.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4 (roles: data manager, table maker, grapher, spokesperson) learners rebuild the evidence pack from their own Lesson 2 to 7 work. (1) Tally the raw list (Learners 1-40) into a frequency table and check the frequencies add to 40: Walk 14, Matatu 12, Boda boda 4, Bicycle 3, Private car 3, School bus 4. (2) Compute percentages (f/n x 100: 35%, 30%, 10%, 7.5%, 7.5%, 10%, sum 100%) and note Walk + Matatu = 26 learners = 65%. (3) State the mode of travel (Walk) and explain why mean and median do not apply to categories. (4) Draw a bar graph (frequency axis from 0, steps of 2, bars equal width with gaps, both axes labelled, title) and a pie chart (9 degrees per learner: 126, 108, 36, 27, 27, 36 = 360). (5) Use the siblings table (mean 83/40 = 2.1, median 2, mode 2) and the Eldoret runner times (mean 109.3 s, median 106 s, mode 105 s; mean 105.8 s without the 130 s time) to show when mean, median and mode agree or differ. (6) Check a truncated-axis version of the bar graph (starting at 2) and calculate the true walk to bicycle ratio of 14:3, about 4.7 times, not 12 times. Groups may use a spreadsheet or app offline for the bar graph or pie chart.
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate with a checklist. Ask: 'Show me where your frequencies add to 40.' 'Which angle did you get for Matatu, and how did you get 108?' 'Why can you not find a mean of travel mode?' Give WAIT TIME of 10 seconds after each question before prompting. Cold-call 3 groups to state their totals check. For stuck groups, point back to the earlier lesson's method without re-teaching: 'Look at your Lesson 2 table, what did we do with the tally marks?' Remind: 'Write mean, never average, and give units: seconds, learners.' Check that no learner names are linked to responses.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence-pack building (data-to-evidence chain): learners physically order the cycle collect, organise, summarise, display, interpret, so they see that each step makes the data more usable than the raw list. Comparing tables, graphs and summaries for the same data shows why representation matters.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: frequencies total 40 and percentages total 100%; pie angles total 360; bar graph axis starts at 0 with labels and title; learner states mode = Walk and explains that mean and median do not apply to categories; learner explains that the runner mean (109.3 s) is pulled up by the 130 s outlier while the median (106 s) represents the group better. Use a 4-item checklist per group: table, summary, graph, caution.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group writes a 5-sentence recommendation for Mr Otieno using the claim-evidence-reasoning pattern. Claim: for example, 'Do not spend the money on a bicycle shed on this evidence; collect whole-school data before deciding on the bus or lunch serving.' Evidence: 14 of 40 walk (35%); 12 of 40 use matatu (30%); together 26 of 40 (65%); only 3 of 40 (7.5%) cycle; 4 of 40 (10%) use the school bus. Reasoning: neither walking nor matatu is more than half, so 'almost everyone walks' and 'most come by matatu' are both wrong; few cycle, so little support for a shed; one class of 40 is a small sample and cannot speak for the whole school; the single 14-seater bus serves the whole school, so Zawadi's claim 'The bus is always full' cannot be confirmed or refuted by 4 learners in one class. Groups then give a 90-second presentation to 'Mr Otieno' (the teacher or a learner in role) and use a rubric to give one 'star' and one 'step' to another group.
framework.teacherMoves: Model one sentence frame: 'The data shows ___ (number and percentage), which means ___, so we recommend ___.' Say: 'Your page must answer Atieno, Brian and Zawadi using numbers, not opinions.' Give WAIT TIME of 15 seconds before each group presents. Cold-call 5 learners to restate another group's evidence: 'Otieno, what number did that group use for matatu? Does it support Brian?' Probe: 'Which graph would you put first for Mr Otieno, bar graph or pie chart, and why?' (Either may be defended; expect bar graph for comparing exact counts and pie chart for showing parts of the whole.) Probe: 'What would change your recommendation?' Press for honest limits: 'What does this class data NOT tell us?' Role-play Mr Otieno asking: 'Can I build the bus route from this?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with peer critique and argument from evidence: forces learners to link every conclusion to a specific number, to state what the data cannot show (sample of one class), and to defend a choice of graph or summary, building the Final Explanation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: recommendations that quote exact anchor numbers; correct statement that neither claim is more than half; correct treatment of Zawadi's claim as untestable with this data; use of 'sample' or 'whole school'; no claim that the data proves a bus route is not needed. Use the rubric levels (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches, Below): Meets requires correct data, correct graph or chart, and accurate interpretation with at most minor errors. Record the level for each group.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the DQB from Lesson 1. In their groups they take each question card, decide whether it is Answered, Partly answered or Still open, and write the evidence from Lessons 1 to 7 on a new card. Example questions: 'Who is right, Atieno or Brian?' (answered: neither; walk 35%, matatu 30%). 'Why does the list look meaningless?' (answered: unorganised raw data; a frequency table organises it). 'Which average should we trust?' (answered: depends on data type; siblings agree at about 2, runner times differ because of one slow time). 'Is the bus always full?' (still open: needs whole-school data on the 14-seater bus). 'Should we build a bicycle shed?' (answered: not on this evidence, 7.5% cycle). New questions are added, such as 'How big a sample is fair?' and 'How can we collect the whole-school data fairly?' Each learner writes a final answer to the driving question on a card.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Go to the board and move each card. Prove it with a number.' Give WAIT TIME of 10 seconds before asking for the reason behind each move. Cold-call 4 learners: 'Brian, which card did you move to Answered? What is your evidence?' Ask: 'Which question is still open, and what data would close it?' Celebrate honest 'still open' cards: 'Good statisticians say what they do not yet know.' Photograph or copy the final DQB for the class record.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: DQB revisiting and sorting (Answered, Partly answered, Open): makes learning visible, ties each question to evidence, and shows that science and statistics progress by turning questions into new data collection.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: every moved card has a number as evidence; learners place the bus question as open or partly open for a correct reason (single 14-seater bus, one class only); at least two new questions about sample size or whole-school collection; individual answers to the driving question mention organising, displaying and interpreting data.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners take out the Lesson 1 draft model of 'how data becomes evidence' and, in a different colour, revise it into a final class model. The final model shows: collect (raw list of 40) to organise (tally and frequency table, total check) to summarise (mode; mean and median for numbers, choose by data type and outliers) to display (bar graph for comparing categories, line graph for change over time, pie chart for parts of a whole, honest axes starting at 0) to interpret (claims checked against numbers) to decision (no shed on this evidence; collect whole-school data before bus or lunch). They add a feedback loop: more data leads to a better decision. Each learner then writes the Final Explanation (6-8 sentences) answering the driving question and explicitly lists three changes between their Lesson 1 model and the final model. They complete the summary table (I observed, I learned, I can explain).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Hold up your Lesson 1 model. What was missing?' Give WAIT TIME of 15 seconds, then cold-call 4 learners to name one change. Prompt: 'Where in your model does the 130 s runner time show up? Where does a truncated axis show up?' Probe: 'How can the same list look meaningless in one form and decisive in another?' Expect answers about tables and charts organising and revealing patterns. Walk around and check that the Final Explanation uses the numbers 14, 12, 26 (65%), 3 (7.5%), 4 (10%) and the mean 109.3 s versus median 106 s, in learners' own words. Collect the Final Explanation and models for assessment, and mark against the rubric.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model comparison (Lesson 1 draft versus final model) and written Final Explanation: learners visibly revise a model with new evidence, which consolidates the full cycle and lets them articulate why the same data seems meaningless raw but decisive when organised and displayed.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for a final model with all five cycle steps in order plus a decision and feedback loop; at least three accurate changes from the Lesson 1 draft; a Final Explanation that (1) says neither claim is more than half, (2) explains why tables and graphs make the data decisive, (3) explains that the best summary or graph depends on the data type and question, (4) recommends no shed on this evidence and whole-school data before bus or lunch, and (5) notes the limit of one class sample. Rubric: Exceeds = all five and creative justification; Meets = all five with minor errors; Approaches = three or four; Below = two or fewer.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, check: Did each group quote exact anchor numbers (14, 12, 26 = 65%, 3 = 7.5%, 4 = 10%) rather than opinions? Did learners treat Zawadi's bus claim as untestable with one class, rather than saying it was disproved? Which groups confused mean with mode, or tried to find a mean of travel categories? Did any pie angles fail to sum to 360, or any bar graph axis start above 0? Which statistics step needs a revisit before the next unit (for example, choosing between mean and median when there is an outlier)? How well did quieter learners contribute through assigned group roles? Plan a follow-up where Grade 10 Green helps design a fair whole-school survey for Mr Otieno.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What did you observe? Write what the raw list of 40 responses looked like, and what the frequency table, bar graph and pie chart for Grade 10 Green showed (Walk 14, Matatu 12, Boda boda 4, Bicycle 3, Private car 3, School bus 4), including the mean, median and mode of the runner times.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What did you learn? Explain how organising, summarising and displaying data turns a messy list into evidence, why neither 'almost everyone walks' nor 'most come by matatu' is right, and why the best summary or graph depends on the data and the question.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: How can you explain the answer to the driving question? Write your Final Explanation for Mr Otieno: what the evidence says about the bicycle shed, school bus and lunch serving, and why he should collect whole-school data before deciding.

reading.title: Bar Graphs, Frequency Tables, and Histograms Practice
Represent Real-World Data Using Bar Graphs, Frequency Tables and Histograms (Flexbook)

FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: Mr Otieno, the principal of Lakeview Senior School in Kisumu, has money for only one option: a school bus route, a bicycle shed or a second lunch serving. In this Final Explanation you will use everything you learned about Grade 10 Green's travel data to answer the driving question: How can we turn a messy list of data from our school into clear evidence that helps our principal make a fair decision? Write your answers in the space under each prompt. Use numbers from the data to back up every claim, give units where needed (learners, seconds), and write the mean as 'mean'. You may use a calculator and a protractor if you need them. Remember that all the data come from one class only.

sections.title: Part 1: From a messy list to a frequency table
sections.prompt:
In Lesson 1, three learners disagreed. Atieno said 'Almost everyone walks', Brian said 'Most of us come by matatu', and Zawadi said 'The bus is always full'. Grade 10 Green collected 40 responses in learner order, but the raw list did not settle the argument.

Here is the frequency table of the same 40 responses:

| Travel mode | Frequency |
|---|---|
| Walk | 14 |
| Matatu | 12 |
| Boda boda | 4 |
| Bicycle | 3 |
| Private car | 3 |
| School bus | 4 |

(a) Explain why the raw list of 40 responses could not settle the claims, but the frequency table can. (b) Work out the percentage for Walk and for Matatu, and the percentage for the two groups together. (c) Use your numbers to decide whether Atieno and Brian are right, and explain what the class data can and cannot tell us about Zawadi's claim.
sections.exemplar:
(a) The raw list is unorganised: the responses are in learner order, so you would have to count every W, M, B, Bi, C and S by eye to compare the groups. The frequency table groups the same 40 responses and gives one number for each travel mode, and the frequencies add to 40 (14 + 12 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 4 = 40), so the groups can be compared quickly.
(b) Percentage = f / n x 100. Walk = 14/40 x 100 = 35%. Matatu = 12/40 x 100 = 30%. Together: 26 of 40 = 65%.
(c) Neither group is more than half (more than 20 learners). Walk is 14 of 40 and Matatu is 12 of 40. So 'Almost everyone walks' and 'Most of us come by matatu' are both wrong, although together they make 65% of the class. Zawadi's claim is about the school's single 14-seater bus serving the whole school. Only 4 of 40 learners (10%) in this class use the bus, so the class count can neither confirm nor refute her claim.

sections.title: Part 2: Choosing a typical value
sections.prompt:
Grade 10 Green also counted the number of siblings each learner has:

| Siblings | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Learners | 5 | 9 | 12 | 8 | 4 | 2 |

An Eldoret club group of 7 runners had these 800 m training times in seconds: 104, 105, 105, 106, 107, 108, 130 (the runner with 130 s had a cold).

(a) Find the mean, median and mode of the siblings data. (b) Find the mean, median and mode of the runner times, giving the mean to 1 decimal place. (c) Why do the three measures agree for siblings but differ for the runner times? Which measure would you use for the runner times, and why? (d) Which measure can you use for the travel mode data, and what is its value?
sections.exemplar:
(a) Total learners = 40. Sum of f x = 0 + 9 + 24 + 24 + 16 + 10 = 83. Mean = 83 ÷ 40 = 2.075, about 2.1 siblings. Mode = 2 siblings (highest frequency, 12). Median: cumulative frequencies are 5, 14, 26, so the 20th and 21st values are both 2, and the median is 2 siblings.
(b) Sum = 765. Mean = 765 ÷ 7 = 109.3 s. Median = 4th value = 106 s. Mode = 105 s.
(c) The siblings data is spread fairly evenly, so the three measures are close (about 2). The runner times have one outlier, 130 s, which pulls the mean up to 109.3 s, higher than six of the seven times. Without it the mean of the other six is 635 ÷ 6 = 105.8 s, while the median hardly changes. So the median (106 s) is the better measure for the runner times because it is not pulled by the outlier.
(d) Travel mode is categories, not numbers, so the mean and median cannot be found. Only the mode can be used: Walk (14 of 40). Note that Walk is the mode but is not a majority.

sections.title: Part 3: Choosing and checking graphs
sections.prompt:
Mr Kamau showed two bar graphs of the same travel data. On one, the frequency axis started at 0. On the other, it started at 2.

(a) Which type of graph is best for the travel data, and which is best for Mama Achieng's mandazi sales at Kibuye market (Mon 40, Tue 45, Wed 42, Thu 50, Fri 65, Sat 30, Sun 20)? Give a reason for each. (b) On the graph where the axis starts at 2, the Walk bar is 12 units tall and the Bicycle bar is 1 unit tall. What does it make walking look like compared with cycling? What is the true comparison from the data? (c) List four things you would check before trusting a graph.
sections.exemplar:
(a) A bar graph is best for the travel data because travel mode is categories, so the bars are separate with equal widths and gaps. A line graph is best for the mandazi sales because they change over time, with days on the horizontal axis and points joined by straight lines. The mandazi line graph peaks on Friday (65) and is lowest on Sunday (20).
(b) With the axis starting at 2, the Walk bar (12 units) looks 12 times the Bicycle bar (1 unit). The true comparison is 14 : 3, so walking is only about 4.7 times as many as cycling. The graph changes how the data looks, not the data itself.
(c) Check that: the frequency axis starts at 0; the scale has equal steps; both axes are labelled and there is a title; for a pie chart, the angles add up to 360 degrees. Also read the numbers on the graph instead of trusting the picture alone.

sections.title: Part 4: Pie chart angles
sections.prompt:
You drew a pie chart of the 40 travel responses.

(a) How many degrees does each learner represent? Show your working. (b) Calculate the angle for Walk and for Matatu. (c) Give one advantage of the pie chart and one advantage of the bar graph for the travel data. (d) What does the pie chart show about the bicycle group, and what does this mean for the bicycle shed?
sections.exemplar:
(a) 360 ÷ 40 = 9 degrees per learner.
(b) Angle = f / n x 360. Walk = 14/40 x 360 = 126 degrees. Matatu = 12/40 x 360 = 108 degrees.
(c) The pie chart shows each group as a share of the whole, so you can see at a glance that neither Walk nor Matatu takes more than half of the circle. The bar graph shows exact counts and is better for comparing close values such as Boda boda 4 and School bus 4.
(d) The Bicycle sector is small: 3 of 40 learners (7.5%), which is 27 degrees. So this class gives little support for building a bicycle shed.

sections.title: Part 5: Your Final Explanation for Mr Otieno
sections.prompt:
Write a short report (about 8 to 10 sentences) for Mr Otieno that answers the driving question: How can we turn a messy list of data from our school into clear evidence that helps our principal make a fair decision?

In your report: (1) describe the steps that turn the raw list into evidence; (2) say what the evidence shows about the three claims; (3) give your advice about the bicycle shed, the school bus route and the second lunch serving; (4) explain one limit of the data and how Mr Otieno should deal with it.
sections.exemplar: Dear Mr Otieno, the raw list of 40 responses from Grade 10 Green could not settle the argument, because it was unorganised. We tallied it into a frequency table (Walk 14, Matatu 12, Boda boda 4, Bicycle 3, Private car 3, School bus 4; total 40) and showed it in a bar graph and a pie chart. The mode of travel is Walk. Walk is 35% and Matatu is 30%. Neither is more than half, so 'almost everyone walks' and 'most of us come by matatu' are both wrong, although together they make 65%. Only 3 of 40 learners (7.5%) cycle, so this class gives little support for a bicycle shed, and we advise no money for a shed on this evidence. Only 4 of 40 (10%) use the school bus, but Zawadi's claim is about the single 14-seater bus serving the whole school, so our class cannot confirm or refute it. The data come from only one class, which is a small sample. We advise collecting the same data from the whole school before you decide between the bus route and the second lunch serving. The best summary or graph depends on the type of data and the question, so check that any graph has an axis starting at 0 before trusting it.

rubric.criterion: Organising data and calculating from tables
rubric.excellent: All percentages, angles, means and medians are correct, with clear working and the frequencies checked against the total.
rubric.proficient: Most calculations are correct with some working shown; one small slip in rounding or working.
rubric.developing: Several calculations are incorrect or have no working; totals are not checked.

rubric.excellent: Chooses mean, median, mode and graph types correctly for each data type, and explains using the outlier and the categorical data.
rubric.proficient: Chooses most measures and graphs correctly with partial reasons.
rubric.developing: Choices are unclear or not linked to the type of data.

rubric.excellent: Uses exact numbers (14 of 40, 35%; 12 of 40, 30%; 65%) to judge each claim, and correctly says the class count cannot test Zawadi's bus claim.
rubric.proficient: Judges the claims with some numbers; the bus claim is mentioned but not fully explained.
rubric.developing: Gives opinions without numbers, or states the claims are right or wrong without evidence.

rubric.excellent: Explains the truncated axis effect (12 times against a true ratio of about 4.7) and lists several correct checks for an honest graph.
rubric.proficient: Explains that the axis can mislead and lists some checks.
rubric.developing: Does not recognise how a graph can mislead.

rubric.excellent: Clear, honest report that links the steps from raw list to evidence, advises no shed, recommends whole-school data, and states the limit of one class.
rubric.proficient: Gives a clear recommendation but misses one step or the limit of the sample.
rubric.developing: Recommendation is unclear or is not supported by the data.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: How can we turn a messy list of data from our school into clear evidence that helps our principal make a fair decision?

lessons.title: Whose Claim Is Right? Launching the Principal's Problem
lessons.observed: What did we observe? We collected 40 responses from Grade 10 Green about main travel mode (Walk, Matatu, Boda boda, Bicycle, Private car, School bus), saw three conflicting claims from Atieno, Brian and Zawadi, and found the long raw list was hard to use to say who is right.
lessons.learned: What did we learn? Raw data is an unorganised list; a claim needs evidence; a long list does not settle an argument by itself, and one class is not the whole school.
lessons.explained: How can we explain it so far? We have data but not yet evidence for Mr Otieno because the list is unorganised. We predict that organising and showing the data will make the answer clearer, but we still need to find out how, and which summary or graph to trust.

lessons.title: Tally and Frequency Tables: Making Sense of the 40 Responses
lessons.observed: We tallied the 40 raw responses from Grade 10 Green and got Walk 14, Matatu 12, Boda boda 4, Bicycle 3, Private car 3, School bus 4, which add to 40. Percentages are Walk 35%, Matatu 30%, Boda boda 10%, Bicycle 7.5%, Private car 7.5%, School bus 10%. For the 30 trees in the Lakeview compound we got Grevillea 12, Cypress 8, Eucalyptus 6, Neem 4.
lessons.learned: A frequency table has the columns Category (or Value), Tally and Frequency. Tally marks are grouped in fives, and the frequencies must add up to the total number of responses. Percentage = f / n x 100. Categorical data (travel mode, tree type) and discrete data (counts such as siblings) can both be organised this way.
lessons.explained: The raw list could not settle the argument, but the table shows Walk (14 of 40, 35%) is the largest group and Matatu (12 of 40, 30%) is second. Neither is more than half, so 'almost everyone walks' and 'most come by matatu' are both wrong, although together they make 26 of 40, which is 65%. Only 4 of 40 use the school bus and 3 of 40 cycle. The table cannot settle Zawadi's claim about the single 14-seater school bus, and one class is a small sample, so we need typical values, graphs and whole-school data before advising Mr Otieno.

lessons.title: Typical Value: Mode and Mean
lessons.observed: The travel table has its highest frequency at Walk (14 of 40, 35%). The siblings table has its highest frequency at 2 siblings (12 of 40). Adding an fx column gives Σfx = 83 for Σf = 40.
lessons.learned: The mode is the value or category with the highest frequency and works for categories and numbers. The mean = Σfx ÷ Σf and works only for numbers. Mean of siblings = 83 ÷ 40 = 2.075, about 2.1 siblings; mode = 2. Travel mode: Walk is the mode but is not a majority.
lessons.explained: The typical Grade 10 Green learner walks to school and has about 2 siblings. The mean (2.1) need not be a whole number because it is a fair share. These summaries describe only this one class, so they are not enough alone to support a decision by Mr Otieno; we need to know when each measure is the best choice (Lesson 4).

lessons.title: Median and Choosing the Best Measure
lessons.observed: We ordered the siblings data and found the 20th and 21st values both equal 2, so the median is 2 siblings (mean 2.1, mode 2). We ordered the 7 Eldoret club 800 m times and found the median 106 s, the mode 105 s and the mean 109.3 s; without the 130 s time the mean of the other six is 105.8 s.
lessons.learned: The median is the middle value of ordered data (for odd n the ((n+1)/2)th value; for even n the mean of the two middle values). One very large or small value (an outlier) pulls the mean but hardly moves the median. For categories such as travel mode only the mode (Walk, 14 of 40) can be used.
lessons.explained: The mean, median and mode agree for the siblings data because it is evenly spread, but they differ for the runner times because one slow time (130 s) pulls the mean up. So the best summary depends on the type of data and the question. For Mr Otieno this means choosing and explaining the measure honestly, and remembering that these data are from only one class.

lessons.title: Bar graphs and line graphs: which picture fits which data?
lessons.observed: Bar graph of travel: Walk 14, Matatu 12, Boda boda 4, Bicycle 3, Private car 3, School bus 4 (total 40), with the tallest bar for Walk. Line graph of Mama Achieng's mandazi sales: Mon 40, Tue 45, Wed 42, Thu 50, Fri 65, Sat 30, Sun 20, peaking on Friday and falling to Sunday.
lessons.learned: A bar graph suits categories, with separate equal-width bars and a frequency axis starting at 0. A line graph suits change over time, with time on the horizontal axis and points joined by straight lines. Both need labelled axes and a title.
lessons.explained: The same table of travel data becomes clear evidence in a bar graph: Walk is 14 of 40 (35%) and Matatu is 12 of 40 (30%), so neither claim shows a majority, though together they are 65%. Bicycle (3 of 40) gives little support for a shed. We should choose the graph that matches the data type, and collect whole-school data before deciding on the bus or lunch serving.

lessons.title: Pie charts: turning frequencies into angles
lessons.observed: We observed that the 40 travel responses can be shown as a pie chart: Walk 126 degrees, Matatu 108 degrees, Boda boda 36 degrees, Bicycle 27 degrees, Private car 27 degrees and School bus 36 degrees, which add up to 360 degrees. Walk takes 14 of 40 learners (35%) and Matatu 12 of 40 (30%), so together 65%, but neither is more than half the circle. We also drew the Wanjiru family budget of KSh 30,000 (Food 144, Rent 90, School fees 54, Transport 36, Savings 36 = 360).
lessons.learned: We learned that angle = f / n x 360, that each learner in our class is worth 9 degrees, that the angles of a pie chart must add up to 360, and that a pie chart shows each part as a share of the whole while a bar graph shows exact counts and is better for comparing close values.
lessons.explained: We can explain that the pie chart helps Mr Otieno see at a glance that walking and matatu are the biggest groups but neither is the majority, and that only 3 of 40 (7.5%) cycle, so this class gives little support for a bicycle shed. Because this is only one class, we advise collecting the same data from the whole school before deciding on the bus or second lunch serving.

lessons.title: Reading Graphs Critically and Using Digital Tools
lessons.observed: We observed that the same travel data looked very different on two bar graphs: with the axis starting at 0, Walk (14) is about 4.7 times Bicycle (3); with the axis starting at 2, Walk looked 12 times Bicycle. We also read the pie chart and the mandazi line graph, and recreated the travel graphs on a spreadsheet or app.
lessons.learned: We learned to read exact values from bar graphs, pie charts and line graphs, to support every conclusion with a number, and to check a graph for a frequency axis that starts at 0, equal steps, labels, a title and pie angles that add to 360. We also learned that one class cannot speak for the whole school.
lessons.explained: A misleading graph changes how the data looks, not the data itself. Honest graphs of the travel data show Walk 14 of 40 (35%) and Matatu 12 of 40 (30%), together 65%, and only 3 of 40 (7.5%) cycling, so the class gives little support for a bicycle shed. Mr Otieno should trust a graph only after checking its axis and scale, and should collect whole-school data before deciding on the bus or lunch serving.

lessons.title: Project: Evidence for the Principal
lessons.observed: What did you observe? Write what the raw list of 40 responses looked like, and what the frequency table, bar graph and pie chart for Grade 10 Green showed (Walk 14, Matatu 12, Boda boda 4, Bicycle 3, Private car 3, School bus 4), including the mean, median and mode of the runner times.
lessons.learned: What did you learn? Explain how organising, summarising and displaying data turns a messy list into evidence, why neither 'almost everyone walks' nor 'most come by matatu' is right, and why the best summary or graph depends on the data and the question.
lessons.explained: How can you explain the answer to the driving question? Write your Final Explanation for Mr Otieno: what the evidence says about the bicycle shed, school bus and lunch serving, and why he should collect whole-school data before deciding.
